P001.research_role: Identified as Jno Miller in the 1860 Baltimore Ward 18 household and as John T. Miller in the 1870 Ward 14 household

confidence_assessment.assessed_proposition: Identified as Jno Miller in the 1860 Baltimore Ward 18 household and as John T. Miller in the 1870 Ward 14 household
confidence_assessment.rationale: The 1870 household, Baltimore painter occupation cluster, 1872 John T. painter marriage, family tradition and later records are now assessed together as a high-confidence identification. The census itself does not print household relationships, and conflicting reported birthplaces remain preserved. The researcher accepts the 1860 Ward 18 boy as the same John Thomas, supported by the later household and the McLaughlin family connection.

evidence.statement: Death certificate: born 17 April 1851 in Washington, D.C.; died 20 November 1938 in Alhambra, Los Angeles County, California; widower of Annah Miller. Blacksmith, retired 1913 after 30 years in occupation. Burial Rose Hill Memorial Park 23 November 1938; informant Asa Miller, 217 Bogart Street, Baldwin Park.
Death certificate names father John Miller, born Germany; mother maiden name unknown, birthplace Devonshire, England. It does not give William Alexander, Abraham, or Blackstone.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: High confidence in reported wording, not in informant accuracy about earlier generations.

evidence.statement: Original marriage register: John T. Miller,22,painter,resident Baltimore City Md, married W. Anna Bruce,17,resident Piedmont WVa,13September1872 at Westernport. Official bestreading Geo.G.Brooke; Date of Record12September1872.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: OriginalS09now inspected; no parents or birthplace fields. Residence not birth. Record date precedes marriage, unexplained, not labeledlicense. Age22 differs from1851birth. Officiant bestGeo.G.Brooke versus derivativeGeorgeW.Brooks; preserve readinghistory. Same event, not independent corroboration.

evidence.statement: 1910: age 59, Anna 56, married 38 years, nine children born/seven living; William and Lula in household. Birthplace overwritten, apparently Washington, D.C.; mother England.
1920: age 68, Washington, D.C.; father New York; mother London, England; Anna 65 Maryland; William 36 Minnesota; Lula 26 Illinois.

Verified working identification: the John T., 18, reportedly Virginia-born, enumerated in the 1870 Baltimore Ward 14 household with John W. and Margaret Miller is John Thomas Miller, the later husband of W. Anna Bruce.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: High-confidence identity conclusion from the combined record set and family evidence. The 1870 census does not state family relationships, so the relationship conclusion is not based on an explicit census label.

evidence.statement: A handwritten family-history account supplied in 2026 identifies John Thomas as the son of John W. A. Miller and Anna Elizabeth Blackstone; says he apprenticed in Baltimore under John William Bruce, lived with the Bruce family while learning blacksmithing, married W. Anna Bruce in 1872 as a Baltimore painter, also painted carriages and made calling cards, and later moved repeatedly with his family before settling in the St. Louis and California areas. An embedded obituary clipping reports his death on 20 November 1938, birth on 17 April 1851 in Washington, D.C., five surviving named children, and Rose Hills burial.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: This is a retrospective family account with an undated, unattributed newspaper clipping. It is direct evidence of the family tradition and useful corroboration where it matches contemporary records, but its individual assertions require separate verification. The PDF's final handwritten note that John came to California in 1938 conflicts with its own clipping saying he had lived in the state for 12 years at death in 1938.

evidence.statement: A Family Group Record lists John Thomas Miller as the child of John William Alexander Miller and Anna Elizabeth Blackstone, born 17 April 1851 in Washington, D.C., married 'William Anna Bruce' on 13 September 1872, and died 20 November 1938.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The birth, marriage and death details closely match independent records and make the sheet useful derivative corroboration. The parentage fields remain family tradition: the post-1964 form is not contemporary, its compiler is unidentified, and its general note 'from John T. Miller' does not specify which entries came from him.

evidence.statement: A user-supplied mounted infant portrait is identified by the user as John Thomas Miller. The visible mount bears the imprint 'Brockmeyer, East St. Louis, Ill.'
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The scan has no visible subject inscription or date. The identification is preserved as family-supplied provenance, but the image does not independently establish the subject or whether the portrait, a copy, and the East St. Louis mount are contemporaneous.

evidence.statement: An album page labels a seated man as John Thomas Miller and the standing woman beside him as Annah Bruce Miller. Its handwritten note repeats John's 17 April 1851 birth and preserves family tradition about his mother's early death, his father's 1856 marriage to Mary E. Lawson, and John's departure from home as a teenager.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The labels are a direct family identification of the pictured couple, but the page does not name its writer, compiler, photographer, or date. The biographical prose is retrospective family tradition and its events, motives, and religious characterization require independent corroboration.

evidence.statement: A review of the posted 1830–1854 Concordia Lutheran Evangelical Church, Washington, D.C., birth/christening transcription found no target John Thomas or John T. Miller in the 1851 entries under Miller/Muller/Mueller variants.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Bounded negative in a derivative transcription that explicitly warns it may be incomplete. The underlying original's 1851–early 1854 baptism leaves were subsequently inspected as S125/E105. This does not show that P001 was never baptized in Washington or in another congregation.

evidence.statement: In the Concordia Lutheran Evangelical Church's original Washington, D.C., baptism register, no John Thomas or John T. Miller baptism, or child of John and Ann/Anna Miller fitting the target, was identified in the January 1851–early 1854 leaves.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Bounded inspection of FamilySearch microfilm 1303264 / DGS 007548824, images 35–41, register pages 52–65, using page images and available machine transcripts. Image 38 names Mary Eva Miller, daughter of Jacob and Hannah Miller, a distinct entry. This does not exclude an overlooked entry, a later baptism, or another congregation. evidence.statement: George Luther Miller delayed certificate reports birth 8 January 1890 at Joliet; father John T. Miller, age 36 (best reading), blacksmith, born Washington D.C.; mother William Annah Bruce, 35, born Baltimore Maryland. evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: High confidence in the principal literal fields; strong correlation to existing P127 via exact name/date/place and S761/S762, no identity merge. evidence.statement: A Baltimore court order of 12 January 1877 pays out a guardianship balance to a John Miller the court says had reached legal age.

evidence.statement: The original Caroline Street Methodist register enters a man named John Thomas Miller as Adult, baptized on 29 June 1868 in Baltimore. The literal reading is secure; identification as P001 remains open.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Baptism supplies no numerical age, birth date or place, parent, address, occupation or spouse. The competing printer and his relationship to the church member are unproved. Book 1 baptism sequence begins in 1857; coverage of early marriages has a 1853–1857 gap. Book 2 baptism and probationer sections read completely; class and later book coverage is selective. Exact visual ledger preserved. No canonical relationship or birth fact changes.

evidence.statement: Every diary spread in FamilySearch item 8 images 589–627 was directly read, covering all displayed entries for 1850 and 1851, with late 1849 and early 1852 context through 9 May 1852. No recognized target. John Thomas baptized 6 October 1850 is identified as infant son of Thomas Johnson, who died 4 February 1851. Mrs. Miller of Parkin near Pratt requested the baptism of Lorenzo Hobs/Hobbs Miller in 1849; both parents’ given names are unstated and the child died in December 1849.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Clergy diary with embedded sacramental entries; no complete tabular 1851 baptism series was located. Some entries do not supply surnames or parents. Earlier part of item 8 and item 9 were sampled for navigation, not read in full. The 1852 manuscript page order differs from date order. No negative beyond the exact diary section.

evidence.statement: 1870 Ward 7 Edward [initial uncertain] Miller, 33, is a gas fitter in a two-person family with Mary; John Miller, 20, is a milk dealer in the Charles Baker household. Neither page gives a street address. The original 1870 directory lists Edward G. gasfitter at 156 E. Monument separately from Edward J. clerk C. H. at 100 S. Caroline, and lists the John T. printer and John currier at 100 S. Caroline. Neither census candidate establishes the Caroline household.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Original census middle initial for Edward is uncertain despite index J; occupation is clear. Occupation correlation to Edward G. is a lead, not a proof. Census does not state relationships. This is a two-candidate comparison, not a full Ward 7 or city census search; the printer’s identity remains open.

evidence.statement: C18948 is John Thomas Miller, an infant born 3 March 1908 in Baltimore, died 21 January 1909 aged 10 months 18 days. Place of death and residence 1003 Green’s Court; father Charles Wm. Miller, mother Maggie Miller informant, maiden surname best read Kline (provisional). No occupation. This is neither P001 nor the adult Caroline Street printer or 1868 baptism recipient.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Original scanned certificate is conclusive for the age-based identity exclusion. Maiden surname remains provisional. No wider collateral relationship is established or excluded. The 1868 adult baptism and the directory printer remain unassigned.

evidence.statement: Four original Baltimore City M indenture indexes produced no supported match for John Thomas Miller. The indexed 1862 John Miller is the earlier Turner case, and Mary Kate Miller is a separate case.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: High confidence in the bounded index readings, not an exhaustive search for a contract or proof no training took place.

evidence.statement: The 1853 Baltimore County Grove A. Shipley contract concerns a John Miller who would turn 21 in April 1865 and was bound to farming; he is a namesake.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Date of birth is inferred from the stated majority date; no parent or birthplace in the contract.

evidence.statement: Baltimore original directories list a John M. Bruce, coppersmith in 1864 and 1867 and at 160 Aisquith through the 1873 listing. No record joins him to John Thomas Miller.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: High confidence in what the entries say; identity as the reported John William Bruce remains unproven.

evidence.statement: The 1860 Washington-born John Miller, nine, enumerated with Adam and Elizabeth Miller, is documented with the same adults in Washington in 1870, age 19 and employed in a restaurant. The 1870 Baltimore census places the project’s John T. in the separate John W. and Margaret Miller household.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: High confidence in the separate census trails. The census does not explicitly state household relationships. The proposed burial linkage is unverified.

evidence.statement: The 1936 DAR typescript of the Rock Creek register contains no identified baptism for John Thomas in the complete copied section. The early sequence jumps from 14 March to 6 July 1851 and from 13 July 1851 to March 1853.
evidence.confidence_level: high for the reading and bounded review
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The DAR manuscript is a 1936 typescript from parish books and verified copies, not an image of original Book A. The original microfilm at MSA SC 4571, SCM 1460-1 item 5 remains unread. April 1851 falls between entries in the transcribed baptism list. No conclusion about whether a baptism occurred or about maternity or the groom’s identity follows from the negative review.

evidence.statement: The 1908 Boston-born Mary Mankin is a likely namesake of the Maryland-born Boyd Street wife. The 1890 directory carries the John W., George L. and Robert L. names to a shared address. A possible George L. estate is indexed in 1910, file 1205, and awaits originals. The 1851 bride remains unproven as John Thomas’s mother and the groom remains unassigned.
evidence.confidence_level: high for original readings, provisional for namesake and household continuity
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The Boyd Street Mary was recorded as age 40 in 1880, implying about age 10–11 at the wedding. The evidence from the Mankin household does not identify the bride. The Joseph Bentley probate index checks and the Advertiser page review have bounded coverage.

evidence.statement: The 5 October 1872 Frostburg Mining Journal, p. 3, lists John T. Miller and W. Anna Bruce among the couples issued marriage licenses by the clerk in September 1872.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The newspaper was published after the 13 September marriage and names no individual issue day. It does not establish that 12 September, the civil register’s Date of Record, was the issue date. The newspaper could derive from the same clerk’s records.

evidence.statement: The 1860 Baltimore Ward 18 return lists Jno Miller, eight, born Maryland, on line 9 of family 4348 with Jno W. and Margaret Miller and the McLaughlans. The researcher identifies this boy as John Thomas Miller.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: On 12 November 2026 the researcher identified the eight-year-old Jno Miller on line 9 as John Thomas Miller. The John W. and Margaret household and the McLaughlin association support the identification, as does the age progression from eight in 1860 to eighteen in 1870. Both census ages are one year younger than the reported 17 April 1851 birth date implies. The 1860 return gives Maryland and the 1870 return gives Virginia, while the later death certificate reports Washington, D.C. The 1860 census supplies no relationships. The six-year-old Thomas on line 10 remains unassigned.

evidence.statement: A handwritten family-history account describes W. confidence_assessment.assessed_proposition: The Baltimore painter, constable, justice of the peace and magistrate is the John W. A. Miller who died in 1877. He is the high-confidence father of John Thomas. The 1851 Baltimore Sun notice identifies Emanuel Miller as his father.
confidence_assessment.rationale: The 1870 Ward 14 household, distinctive initials, painter trade, directory and public-office continuity, family tradition, the 1877 painter death record and the shared Western Cemetery plot with Margaret are assessed together as a verified working identity. Conflicting reported age and birthplace remain documented but no longer keep these records as separate identities. Emanuel’s 1851 first-person statement gives a father and an approximate 1832 birth, in conflict with the Abraham tradition and the age in John’s death certificate. The researcher also accepts the 1860 Ward 18 household as John and Margaret’s. The McLaughlin co-residence gives a link through Charlotte, identified as his sister in the later reports.

evidence.statement: District of Columbia marriage registers record John W. A. Miller and Mary M. M. Lawson on 18 February 1856. The chronological volume headed Marriage Licenses establishes the license context. The handwritten initial is W.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The original images verify the license record and W. A. initials. A separate ceremony return and evidence of either party’s parents remain unrecovered.

evidence.statement: Family identifies the expanded name as John William Alexander; individual records usually say John W. A.
1864 painter, 135 Raborg; 1867 painter, 129 Raborg.

On 5 December 1867 the Baltimore City Orphans’ Court bound Mary Kate Miller, aged sixteen, to a man recorded as John W. A. Miller until she turned eighteen. He agreed to provide maintenance, clothing and instruction in reading, writing, plain sewing and housework, and to pay $30 at the end of the term.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The original verifies the indenture and the master’s name. Matching initials, date and city suggest a possible association with P003. The record supplies no address, occupation, parent names or stated kinship.

evidence.statement: Maryland House of Delegates journal, 5 March 1868, pp.652-653, names Ward 14 John W. A. Miller among 1867 constable appointees; resolution addresses $2 commission refunds after commissions were pronounced void.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Page header Mar.5 dates the action; March 30 is in the volume catalog title. Mr. Mullin offered a resolution naming Ward 14 John W. Pierce and John W. A. Miller among 1867 constable appointees who qualified and paid $2 commissions. Page 653 states the Court of Appeals ruled commissions void and proposes refunds on demand; first reading only. Does not establish valid commissions, enactment or continuous tenure.

evidence.statement: 1868–69 directory: John W. A. Miller, constable, office 518 W. Baltimore, dwelling 129 Raborg. The 1870 directory prints him twice as constable: at 129 Raborg, and with an office at Baltimore/Paca and dwelling at 660 W. Baltimore.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Both digitized printed pages were visually checked in 2026. The 1868 dwelling corroborates continuity with the 1867 painter at 129 Raborg. The duplicate 1870 entries do not establish when an address changed or imply two people. Neither page names his spouse or child.

evidence.statement: 1872 original directory lists John W. A. Miller, constable, 660 w Balto;1873 constable and1874 magistrate at same listed address.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: 1872 printedp424 now directly visually verified8November2026; no dw qualifier, office need not be home. Prior1873/1874checks retained. No new familyidentitybridge.

evidence.statement: Verified working identification: the 1870 Ward 14 John W., 37, Virginia-born house painter, enumerated with Margaret, 37, and John T., 18, is Baltimore John W. A. Miller.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The census does not print relationships. Identification is based on the correlated household, occupation, location, directories, family evidence and later records.

evidence.statement: Verified working identification: the Baltimore painter, constable and magistrate is the John W. A. Miller whose death certificate records death on 27 November 1877 and Western Cemetery burial. The 1909 Margaret Miller certificate gives father Lawson and Georgetown, D.C., origin, and her memorial records the same Western Cemetery plot 307-H.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The John W. A. death-record identity is verified at high confidence from the combined evidence. No single record resolves every age or birthplace conflict, and the separate Mary M. M. Lawson given-name question remains open.

evidence.statement: Exact FamilySearch cataloging establishes that the Charles T. Zahn translation of Zion Lutheran Middletown includes baptisms through 1827, and that the indexed Christ Reformed Middletown typescript includes baptisms through 1840. Both therefore cover the death-derived c.1824-1825 target window.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: This is high-confidence coverage and access-path evidence, not evidence that John appears in either register. The authenticated digital films are restricted to a FamilySearch Center or affiliate library and were not readable from home.

evidence.statement: The age-compatible 1850 Washington County John Miller candidates reviewed do not furnish a parent Abraham. Jno, 25, was in Jacob Miller's household; John, 27, was in Henry C. Miller's household; and John D., 25, in the McCoy household remains unconnected. John W., 29, with Sarah/Sahara and two young children was traced forward: he remained with Sarah A. and their child sequence in Clear Spring in 1860 and 1870, overlapping the target's 1856 marriage and verified 1870 Baltimore household.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: An earlier wife and child are not disqualifying because family tradition places John Thomas with Anna Elizabeth Blackstone before Mary/Margaret. This particular John W. is excluded by later continuity with Sarah, not by the mere existence of a pre-1856 family. The survey is not a countywide absence proof; census household membership does not itself prove relationships, and the target may have been elsewhere, omitted, or differently indexed.

evidence.statement: Original Frederick probate records now directly connect the two leading Frederick household clues: on 5 January 1836 Susanna Miller and Jacob T. C. Miller bonded as administrators of Abraham Miller, with Leonard Miller and George Main as additional obligors. Later inventories and the final account repeat Susanna and Jacob T. C. as administrators of Abraham, late of Frederick County.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: This elevates the Frederick Abraham/Leonard network above the Washington County candidate because it combines the reported birthplace, Abraham tradition and a direct Abraham-Leonard association. It does not name John, state kinship, or resolve why Abraham's own 1830 household lacked a boy age 5-9 while Leonard's had one.

evidence.statement: Frederick land indexes now add a property network to the probate association: Abraham and Leonard Miller each had adjacent-year transactions involving Jacob Grove, a probable Jacob T. C. Miller entry later involved Jacob Grove Sr., and Abraham-estate purchasers George W. and Daniel Miller subsequently conveyed or transacted directly with administrator Jacob T. C. Miller.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: This materially strengthens the conclusion that Abraham, Leonard, Jacob T. C., George W., and Daniel belonged to one close property/estate network. It still does not name John, prove any kinship, or explain why the age-matched boy was in Leonard's rather than Abraham's 1830 household. Original deeds are the next decisive records. Original follow-up29 September2026 is recorded in the newly added deed assessment below.

evidence.statement: No target-age John Miller was identified in a bounded review of relevant Frederick Orphans Court proceedings, guardian indexes, or Orphans Bound records as a child formally transferred from Abraham's estate to Leonard.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: This is a scoped negative only. It does not exclude informal fostering, residence with relatives before Abraham's death, missed OCR or spelling, or unindexed loose material.

evidence.statement: In 1846 Jacob T. C. Miller administered Susan Miller's Frederick County estate, whose inventory included Nance and her child, closely paralleling Nancy and child in Abraham Miller's 1836 inventory. The administration surety was written as John Miller 'of H.'
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Estate-household continuity strongly supports the Abraham/Susan/Jacob association without explicit kinship. The surety John of H. is not identified as target John; neither the recovered1846/1859 deeds nor the cited equity abstract identifies his father as Henry. See dated correction and S190/S202/S204.

evidence.statement: A handwritten family-history account begins by calling John William Alexander Miller the son of Abraham Miller, born about 1825 in Washington, D.C., and husband of Anna Elizabeth Blackstone. A later note on the same page says the writer had since learned that John W. A. was born in Germany and then assumes he married Anna in England.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: This newly preserved artifact may explain how the Abraham tradition was transmitted, but it supplies no contemporary record or named informant for the parentage claim. Its Washington, D.C., and Germany birth statements conflict with each other and with the Maryland/Virginia evidence already retained. The inferred English marriage is explicitly an assumption in the manuscript, not a documented event.

evidence.statement: A Family Group Record names John William Alexander Miller, reports birth about 1828 in Washington, D.C., places 'About 1898' in his burial-date field, names his father Abraham Miller, identifies Anna Elizabeth Blackstone as wife, and lists Mary M. M. Lawson as another wife with the date 18 February 1856.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The sheet is a derivative family compilation on a form printed no earlier than 1964. A general source note says 'from John T. Miller,' but it does not attribute individual fields. The Abraham entry documents the family tradition, not original-record parentage. The 1856 date matches the independently verified D.C. registers; the c.1828 Washington birth and c.1898 burial conflict with stronger records placing his death in Baltimore on 27 November 1877.

evidence.statement: Open 1851 and 1858-1859 Baltimore city directories and 1860, 1862 and 1864 Washington-Georgetown directories were searched for John W. A. Miller, John W. Miller and painter variants. No target entry was identified before the established 1864 Baltimore painter entry.

evidence.statement: A broad Library of Congress search surfaced Der Deutsche Correspondent of 28 November 1877, page 4, as a possible John Miller lead for the day after John W. A. Miller's death.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: No target notice has been visually verified or translated. The page is preserved only as a search lead and is not evidence that an obituary appeared.

evidence.statement: The John W. Miller farmer enumerated in Berkeley County, Virginia, in 1850 and 1860 continues with overlapping household members in Hedgesville, Berkeley County, West Virginia, in 1870 and is still alive there as a farmer with wife Margaret and children in the original 1880 census. He is a distinct namesake, not the Baltimore John W. A. Miller who died 27 November 1877.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The four Berkeley census images show strong continuity through repeated spouse/child names, ages, place and farmer trade. The 1880 living Berkeley man cannot be the Baltimore man who died in 1877. The 1860 Berkeley boy John N. and the 1870 Berkeley farm worker John are not identified as P001 by shared name and age; no relationship between the lines is established.

evidence.statement: A Baltimore City Archives WPA name-index card headed John W. A. Miller refers to an 1859 coroner-inquest record, HRS 104, and a 1874 Belair Market armory petition, HRS 717.

Neither underlying document was examined, and the card provides no occupation, address, family relationship, or role in the inquest or petition. It does not establish P003 in Baltimore in 1859 or connect the 1860 Ward 18 huckster household (occupation corrected by original review8November2026).

evidence.statement: A contemporary Baltimore newspaper notice dated 1 July 1855 names Ottomar Brehme and John W. Miller as founders of Brehme, Miller & Co., an importing and commission dry goods firm at 20 German Street.

It omits the A. initial, relatives, painter trade, and a later address bridge. Association with P003 is a research lead only; no biographical fact is assigned to P003 from this notice.

evidence.statement: A Baltimore City male marriage-index card names John W. Miller and E. Doras Hayes, issue date 9 October 1858. P065.research_role: Washington County farmer formerly considered for the Abraham in the family papers.

confidence_assessment.assessed_proposition: A Washington County Abraham appears in the 1820 and 1830 censuses and likely in 1850. His identity and any connection to Emanuel’s family remain open.
confidence_assessment.rationale: The household ages support continuity, and later deeds naming Abraham and Catharine give a property lead. The 1830 schedule leaves the children unnamed. Emanuel’s 1851 notice (S2249) supersedes the earlier proposed fatherhood of this Abraham.

evidence.statement: In 1820 an Abraham Miller headed a Washington County District 1 household with a male age 26-44, a female 16-25 and a boy under 10. Seven enslaved people were also enumerated and the head was engaged in agriculture.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The schedule names only the head. The substantial enslaved household should make this man traceable through tax, land and probate records.

evidence.statement: In 1830 a Washington County District 1 Abraham, age 40-49, headed a ten-person household containing one boy age 5-9, an exact age-slot match for John if born about 1824-1825.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The unnamed boy is only compatible with John, not identified as him. The head's age progression from the 1820 Washington schedule is plausible but does not prove continuity.

evidence.statement: The only indexed Washington County Abraham located in the reviewed 1840 search was a younger Clear Spring head age 20-29, not the older 1820-1830 man.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: This is only an index-level gap. The later discovery of an age-compatible Abraham in Washington County in 1850 supersedes the earlier suggestion that the older head probably died or moved before 1840. The younger man may be a relative, but that has not been proved.

evidence.statement: In 1850 a Maryland-born Abraham Miller, age 62, headed a Subdivision 2 Washington County household, worked as a farmer and reported $13,000 in real estate. The household included Catharine 52; Jacob 30; Joseph 20; Benjamin 15; Elizabeth 26; Mary 20; Catharine 18; Martha 12; and Ellen Null 12.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The original schedule clearly reads Abraham's age as 62, producing a birth estimate about 1788 compatible with the 1830 head. The census does not state relationships. Several age slots can be reconciled with the 1830 household, but the match is imperfect and does not prove same-person continuity. An adult son born about 1824-1825 could already have left the household by 1850.

evidence.statement: A Washington County probate general index records administration for an Abraham Miller on 10 October 1865. A Herald and Torch Light legal notice eight days later called for claims against Abraham Miller's estate and indexed Joseph Garver as the associated person.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The existence, date and county of the estate are independently corroborated. S81 now confirms Joseph Garver and the bond itself. The index and article abstract do not name heirs, state a death date, or prove this was the Abraham age 62 in 1850. The inventory, sale, accounts and any distribution remain to be recovered. Correction, 1 October 2026: the recovered will S352 and final account S353 name widow Nancy; the younger Cavetown/Ringgold cluster P109 probably identifies this estate. Retained as historical investigation, not evidence of P065’s death or kinship. The account clarifies John S. Newcomer and George Fulton as appraisers.

evidence.statement: The Washington County probate, land and chancery access survey identifies the exact archival series needed to test this candidate. No Abraham Miller case was found in the public 1782-1851 chancery index, while the relevant land indexes and several probate series require center/affiliate or archive access.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: This establishes record coverage and a bounded chancery negative, not a negative result for probate, deeds or guardianships. Restricted records were not bypassed. On 1 October 2026, lawful Maryland LandRec access independently supplied originals S356 and S358–S361; FamilySearch restrictions were not bypassed.

evidence.statement: The original Washington County bond volume index sends Miller, Abraham to volume G, page 430. The 10 October 1865 bond names Joseph Garver, Isaac Garver and Christian Newcomer as obligors and conditions Joseph Garver's service for Abraham Miller's estate.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: This confirms the estate representative and two bondsmen and proves the estate entry is not merely an index abstraction. It names no heirs or kinship, does not identify John, and does not by itself prove that the decedent was the 1850 Abraham. Joseph and Isaac Garver and Christian Newcomer are now priority associates for neighborhood, deed and kinship reconstruction. Correction, 1 October 2026: the recovered will S352 and final account S353 name widow Nancy; the younger Cavetown/Ringgold cluster P109 probably identifies this estate. Retained as historical investigation, not evidence of P065’s death or kinship. The account clarifies John S. Newcomer and George Fulton as appraisers.

evidence.statement: The Washington County inventory warrant for Abraham Miller was issued 10 October 1865. John S. Newcomer and probably George Fulton appraised the personal estate and signed on 14 October; Joseph Garver, executor, affirmed it on 17 October. The total appraisement was $468.14 and included domestic furnishings, bedding, food stores, tools, two hogs and a cow.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: This original record confirms the same estate sequence and expands the associate network. It names no widow, child, heir or buyer and gives no residence below Washington County. The second appraiser's surname is difficult; the original and inconsistent OCR support a provisional reading of Fulton. Correction, 1 October 2026: the recovered will S352 and final account S353 name widow Nancy; the younger Cavetown/Ringgold cluster P109 probably identifies this estate. Retained as historical investigation, not evidence of P065’s death or kinship. The account clarifies John S. Newcomer and George Fulton as appraisers.

evidence.statement: Derivative cemetery memorials identify estate executor Joseph Garver and bondsman Isaac Garver as brothers buried at Welty Church of the Brethren Cemetery and identify Isaac's wife as Fannie Newcomer. This supplies a plausible pre-existing Garver-Newcomer family or community network for Christian Newcomer's role on Abraham's 1865 bond.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The memorial relationships are derivative and require original marriage, church, burial and probate verification. They do not establish that Garver or Newcomer was related to Abraham Miller or that Abraham belonged to the Welty congregation. Correction, 1 October 2026: the recovered will S352 and final account S353 name widow Nancy; the younger Cavetown/Ringgold cluster P109 probably identifies this estate. Retained as historical investigation, not evidence of P065’s death or kinship. The account clarifies John S. Newcomer and George Fulton as appraisers.

evidence.statement: The 1821 heir Abraham had wife Catharine; 1854 Abraham/Catharine farm sales beside Daniel’s inherited parcel provide a promising older farmer property hypothesis, P110.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: P065=P110 remains unproved. Wife’s first name, wealth and county fit; deed ages and children are absent. No named target John.

evidence.statement: The 1865 estate formerly pursued for this candidate now has a recovered will and final account naming Nancy. Abraham 25/Nancy 23 in 1860 and an age-31 death in September 1865 probably identify a different man, P109.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Withdraw the former same-generation estate claim. The younger cluster is probable, with an exact census/burial/probate bridge unresolved. No will children does not prove childlessness.

evidence.statement: Bounded 1860 county index searches did not identify the older Abraham or Catharine born about 1798 in Maryland; later land entries involve multiple Abraham namesakes.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Not proof of death or departure. Palmyra Iowa’s age-compatible man was deprioritized through derivative Ohio/Margaret continuity, S362; not assigned to P065.

evidence.statement: Inherited farm deed FF446–448 strengthens P110’s 1821→1854 property continuity. Selected later Abraham transactions belong to church trustee, business and competing Catharine clusters without proven older census identity.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: P065=P110 remains a hypothesis; target parentage low. Original 1860 Conococheague Abraham 51 Pennsylvania/Catharine 42 is separate from 1850 farmer 62 Maryland/Catharine 52.

evidence.statement: Following possible1850householdchildren did not produce a naming bridge: SharpsburgBenjamin/Matilda isdeprioritized by probable1900PA1829identity;IllinoisAbraham/Catharine has substantialhouseholdage/birthplace mismatches;FunkreleaseAbraham belongs younger generation.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: No complete1850childlist proved. Benjaminparentage claim derivative;Illinoisnotcategoricallyexcludedbyagealone. Fulltextselectedhitsnotexhaustive. P065retainedlowasfather.

relationships.basis: Contemporaneous same-name heads in adjacent Maryland counties; no kinship or same-person continuity established.

conflicts_and_cautions: Washington County had been legally separate from Frederick County since 1776, so an 1824-1825 Washington birth would not literally be a Frederick County birth. Informant error or broader regional memory is possible but must not be assumed.
The 1820 household held seven enslaved people while the 1830 household listed none. This change does not prevent continuity but requires tax, deed or probate corroboration.
The 1830-to-1850 household reconstruction is plausible but imperfect; the census schedules before 1850 name only the head and the 1850 schedule states no relationships.

Do not merge this man with the 1820-1830 Frederick County Abraham, the 1840 Clear Spring Abraham, the c.1809 Pennsylvania-born Conococheague miller, or the 1791 Berkeley County Abraham without direct evidence.
1 October 2026: the 1865 Nancy estate probably belongs to younger P109, superseding the former same-generation lead.
P110’s 1821 Catharine couple and probable 1854 seller may be this census farmer, but are not merged. Catharine Rench is unsupported; no exact birth or death adopted.
The neighboring Daniel 71/Michael 50 in 1850 are not proved P080/P079; adjacency does not establish kinship.
S2249 directly names Emanuel as John W. A.’s father. This dossier’s former direct father hypothesis is retained as research history.
unresolved_questions: Can the 1820, 1830 and 1850 censuses be proved the same head and connected to P110’s deeds?
What are the older Abraham and Catharine’s death/migration records after the 1854 sales?
Which 1850 household members were children, and who was the unnamed 1830 boy aged 5–9?
Can a household member be traced to Frederick, Washington D.C. or Baltimore before 1856?
next_research_actions: Prioritize original John Miller probate underlying1821heirs/property and systematic olderAbraham tax/neighbor continuity; seek an original naming1850Jacob,Joseph,Mary,Catharine,Martha withparents. Benjamin/Matilda and Illinois guesses have lower priority afterS378–S383.
Correlate recovered 1821 FF446–448 inherited farm with 1850 household through systematic taxes/neighbor deeds and John Miller probate. Seek records explicitly naming older Abraham’s children.
Identify children through church and guardianship records, especially the unnamed 1830 boy aged 5–9; require a direct bridge before asserting target parentage.
Trace the 1850 younger household members through marriages, church, probate and later censuses; the 1860 Sharpsburg Benjamin blacksmith is an unproved lead.
Search 1823–1827 baptisms using John/Johann/Johannes/Wilhelm/Alexander and Miller variants once the farm and congregation are identified.
Check older-couple death, land and tax records for 1854–1860. A county index miss alone does not prove death.
Resolve 1864 Fouke Abraham/Catharine through 1843 OHW2:117–119 and intervening interests; do not use it as P065 survival before separation from P111.

incoming.basis: Older property-owning farmer and Catharine in 1850 plausibly match the 1821/1854 couple. Wife, wealth and region align, without a direct census-to-deed bridge or deed ages.

P066.preferred_name: Abraham Miller (Frederick County head and probate candidate)
P066.research_role: Middletown property owner whose estate was administered in 1836.

confidence_assessment.assessed_proposition: The 1860 deed names six children of the Middletown Abraham. His relationship to Emanuel and Leonard remains open.
confidence_assessment.rationale: Abraham, Emanuel, and Leonard were separately named buyers at the 1831 Herring estate sale. Leonard signed Abraham’s 1836 administration bond. The 1860 heir deed omits Emanuel and John, both then alive. The deed concerns a specific property, and no record names a family relationship between Abraham and either man. Emanuel’s 1851 notice identifies him as John’s father.

evidence.statement: The 1820 Frederick District 4 head age 45 or older and the 1830 District 3 head age 50-59 form a plausible, though unproved, progression for a man born about 1770-1775.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: District numbering and unnamed households prevent proof of continuity.

evidence.statement: The 1830 Frederick household had no male age 5-9, while Leonard Miller's separate household on the same page had one.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: This weakens a normal resident-father hypothesis but does not exclude a child fostered or living elsewhere.

evidence.statement: The original 5 January 1836 administration bond names Susanna Miller and Jacob T. C. Miller as administrators of Abraham Miller, deceased, with Leonard Miller and George Main as additional obligors on the $2,000 bond.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: This is the first original record directly joining the Frederick Abraham estate to Leonard Miller and strongly corroborates the derivative Susanna/Jacob T. C. family cluster. It states no relationships and does not identify John.

evidence.statement: January and March 1836 inventories and the 1839 first and final account repeatedly identify Susanna Miller and Jacob T. C. Miller as administrators of Abraham Miller, late of Frederick County.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The account confirms Frederick County residence but closes without a distribution to named heirs. The property inventory includes an enslaved woman named Nancy and a child; it names no family relationships or John.

evidence.statement: A derivative 1802 list identifies a Frederick County constable called Abraham Miller, junior, appointed in 1801 and dismissed in 1802.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The age window could fit the later census head, but no record chain proves they were the same man. Junior indicates another older namesake, not necessarily his father.

evidence.statement: At Abraham Miller's public estate sale on 6 February 1836, recurring purchasers included administrator Jacob T. C. Miller, Susanna or Susan Miller, Daniel Miller, George or George W. Miller, Elizabeth Miller and Mary Hedges.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The repeated Miller purchasers form a strong household or close-kin cluster, and Jacob's administrator role plus repeated purchases substantially strengthen the hypothesis that he was Abraham and Susanna's reported son. The sale does not label any purchaser as a child, sibling or other relative. A purchaser machine-read as 'Leo M. Miller' cannot yet be identified as Leonard from the low-resolution handwriting.

evidence.statement: Creagerstown Lutheran christening indexes name Abraham Miller and Susanna or Sussanna as parents of Johannes, born in 1795, and Anna Maria, born in 1797.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The parent-child statements are explicit in the indexes and independently establish an Abraham-Susanna family at Creagerstown. Correlation to the 1820-1830 census head and 1836 decedent is strong but not yet proved. If it is the same couple, their earlier son Johannes is negative evidence against adding the target John without a death or other explanation.

evidence.statement: Frederick land indexes place Abraham Miller in a 15 March 1830 transaction with Jacob Grove Sr.; Leonard Miller in a probable 28 May 1831 transaction with Jacob Grove; and a name appearing to be Jacob T. C. Miller in a 19 July 1833 transaction with Jacob Grove Sr. Later indexes clearly record George W. Miller to Jacob T. C. Miller on 22 April 1839 and Daniel Miller to Jacob T. C. Miller on 21 January 1842.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The repeated Grove connection directly associates Abraham, Leonard and probable Jacob T. C. in one property network. The later George W. and Daniel transactions are especially significant because both names recur as purchasers at Abraham's 1836 estate sale. This strengthens a family or tightly connected property-group interpretation but states no relationship; the original deeds must establish direction, consideration, parcel continuity, spouses, and any inheritance language. Original follow-up29 September2026 is recorded in the newly added deed assessment below.

evidence.statement: A bounded survey of 1834-1838 Orphans Court proceedings, the guardian-bond/account index, and Orphans Bound did not identify a young John Miller placed from Abraham's estate or Leonard's household, nor an exact target-cluster guardianship.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: This makes a formal, indexed orphan-court transfer from Abraham to Leonard less evident, but it does not exclude informal residence, missed spelling, OCR failure, an unindexed order, or loose papers. One GME7 John Miller was an adult guardian of Ramsburg minors and is not the target child.

evidence.statement: On 30 November 1846 Jacob T. C. Miller bonded as administrator of Susan Miller, late of Frederick County, with John Miller 'of H.' and Henry G. Waters as sureties. Susan's December inventory included an enslaved woman called Nance and her child, closely paralleling the Nancy and child in Abraham Miller's January 1836 inventory.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Estate-household continuity strongly supports the Abraham/Susan/Jacob association without explicit kinship. The surety John of H. is not identified as target John; neither the recovered1846/1859 deeds nor the cited equity abstract identifies his father as Henry. See dated correction and S190/S202/S204.

evidence.statement: A 2010 Windsor forum compilation transcribes a 3 July 1890 Frederick Daily News obituary identifying Daniel Miller as brother of Jacob T. C. Miller, George W. Miller, Mary M. Hedges and Mrs. Harrison Feete. Its transcribed 1880 Feete household lists Daniel of A. as brother-in-law and Elizabeth A. as Harrison’s wife.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The unusual sibling-name cluster matches names already present in Abraham’s 1836 estate sale (S86) and subsequent Daniel/George W. transactions with Jacob (S89). This is a promising explicit sibling claim, conditional on original newspaper verification. Elizabeth A. Miller Feete is a new collateral candidate for the estate-sale Elizabeth, not an assigned identity. The compiler separately calls Daniel son of Abraham and Susanna Creager, but the quoted obituary does not name either parent and cannot prove Susan’s maiden name or Valentine parentage. The impossible 1906 birth year and apparent stray 1880 census row require originals. No Ohio/NJ Creagar common ancestor or target John relationship established.

evidence.statement: Robert Fry’s 2002 forum reply names Jacob T. C. Miller siblings Mary M. (wife of Shadrach Hedges), Daniel, George W., Elizabeth A. (wife of J. Harrison Feete), and Jane A.; reports Jacob wife Mary Ann Levy, daughter of Jonathan; and proposes a conjectural Abraham Miller/Hutzell ancestry.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The named siblings align with the 1890 obituary transcription (S182) and original estate/land cluster (S86/S89), adding Jane A. and spouse names as useful discriminators. The forum has no original citations, and underlying independence from other reconstructions is unknown. Hutzell ancestry is expressly unconfirmed by the writer and is not adopted as parentage. Parent post S185 expands Mary to Magdalene, whereas S87 indexes Anna Maria; do not merge these names without originals. The 2000 post supplies the already reported 16 July 1846 Susan death date without a Kentucky place, but neither date nor derivation is verified. No link to target John or NJ/Ohio Creagar common ancestor established.

evidence.statement: The published1790 Frederick census transcription lists Abraham Miller onp60 with counts3,0,3,0,0 and a separate Abraham Miller Senr. onp64 with5,1,7,0,0. Valentine Cregar appears onp63 with2,1,2,0,0.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: High confidence in the printed readings, not identity. Column order: males16+, males under16, females all ages, other free persons, enslaved people. No household members named beyond heads, no relationships. Senr. distinguishes a same-name man but does not prove father-son relationship. Neither Abraham assigned to the later Susan/Jacob estate family or Fry’s proposed Hutzell pedigree. Published list contains alphabetic runs; adjacency does not prove neighbors.

evidence.statement: Original Rocky Hill Lutheran baptism entry114 names Susana/Susanna, daughter of Valentin Krüger and wife Christina, born22 February1773 and baptized22 March1773; sponsors Michael Krüger and wife Margaretha.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Replaces derivative-only birth/baptism parentage with direct original church evidence for the baptizee. Exact surname letter forms merit specialist review; normalized Krüger/Creager. Mother called Christina only. Does not yet establish that this child became Abraham Miller wife Susan, identify sponsor kinship, or connect to Ohio/NJ Creagars. No relationship assertions promoted. Original entry84 additionally names Valentin/Christina son Georg and sponsors Georg Krüger/Catharina; entry14 names sponsors Conrad Krüger/Anna Maria. These are association leads, not sibling proof. Entry14 overwritten child-name line and apparent24-versus-blog17 February1768 discrepancy retained for review.

evidence.statement: Original deeds show Abraham purchased a Grove parcel in1830, Leonard purchased a separate Grove lot in1831, and Jacob T. C.’s1833 lot adjoined Leonard’s. In1839 George W. and wife Elizabeth conveyed Jacob their one-sixth interest in the house and lot Abraham owned when he died. Daniel of A.’s1842 instrument was a debt-security trust of personal property.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Direct property and estate associations support the cluster. None of these records identifies target John as Abraham’s child or explicitly calls George, Daniel or Jacob his sons. One-sixth interest does not alone enumerate six children.

evidence.statement: Recovered Susannah’s first account TS3:99–100,7 February1849, names Jane A. Miller as owner of a bed incorrectly inventoried and includes a judgment expense involving Daniel and Susan Miller. It ends with a balance due the estate.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: No named distributees or target John appear; no widow, son or sibling relationships are stated. Jane’s ownership is consistent with a household association but not proof of Fry’s sister claim.

evidence.statement: Leonard and Charlotte sold their Middletown lot to John Miller of H. for $100 on24 December1846,WBT3:512–513. John of H. and wife Susannah sold the same parcel to Ellen Smith for $600 on20 June1859,BGF4:276; the latter explicitly cites the1846 deed.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The chain is original-record verified, but H. is unexpanded; neither deed identifies John’s father, age, trade or Baltimore residence. Buyer remains an unassigned control lead, not identified with P005 or P003. Earlier Henry fatherhood assertions were unsupported by the cited abstract.

evidence.statement: Selected early court and indenture originals produced other Johns: an adult butcher master in1829 and a1828 ward John whose mother was Catharine Miller.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Neither identified as P005. Bounded full-text searches did not establish a placement from Abraham or Leonard; OCR and selected-page review cannot prove absence.

evidence.statement: The9 February1802 George Beckenbaugh estate debt list names Abraham Miller Sr., Abraham Miller Jr., Valentine/Thomas/Adam Creager and Leonard Miller.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: High confidence in names as recorded, not identities. These people owed the same estate; the record does not establish transactions between them, kinship, Susanna’s maiden name, or Sr./Jr. father-son status. Namesakes remain unassigned to the later1836 Abraham/1846 Susan cluster.

evidence.statement: HS15:323–324 directly names deceased Abraham Miller as father of Daniel Miller of A., who assigned his inherited Middletown house/lot interest to Jacob T. C. Miller as trustee on1 February1842.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Father named Abraham is explicit; attribution to P066’s1836 estate/Grove parcel is correlated through Middletown, deceased Abraham, Daniel and Jacob, but the new deed omits acreage and earlier title reference. No mother, maiden name, brother relationship, complete heir list or John W. A. bridge.

evidence.statement: Susannah’s second and final account2 January1854 carries forward the1849 residue and exhausts it through debt, fees and further administrator commission, without an heir distribution.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Hedges payment is on a note, not a bequest or child share; account does not state kinship, maiden name or John parentage.

evidence.statement: Follow-up to Daniel’s1842 father-Abraham deed found a later Daniel of A.–Eliza Ann Windsor couple and Hedges/Jacob/Feete associations, but did not trace the inherited Middletown share or name additional heirs.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: These are collateral correlations only. Father attribution to this1836 Abraham, Daniel’s mother, full heir group and target John parentage remain unproved.

evidence.statement: Selected later land-index follow-up found Jacob T. C. Miller’s1860 Wheaton trust and Brown mortgage; neither supplies the inherited Abraham house title or a John W. A. connection.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Limited to selected index pages and the inspected instruments. Wheaton’s title derives from Ramsburgh in Hilliers Addition. No comprehensive absence or new relationship assertion.

evidence.statement: Wentz1920 explicitly names Abram as father of Mary Magdalen Miller Hedges; Daniel’s original1890obituary establishes her Miller sibling group.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: This supports a specific collateral family hypothesis; it does not identify the biographical Abram with this canonical Abraham, establish Susan/Creager as mother, or connect targetJohn. SAR depends on Wentz and adds no maternal grandfather identity.

evidence.statement: BGF5:697–698, executed 9 June 1860 and recorded 22 June, directly names deceased intestate Abraham Miller’s children/heirs: Mary M. Hedges, Jacob T. C. Miller, Daniel Miller of A., George W. Miller, Elizabeth A. Feete and Jane A. Miller. Jane died intestate without issue; her share descended to her brothers and sisters. The deed explicitly recites the 1830 Grove-to-Abraham purchase JS33:443.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Direct children of the Abraham property owner and direct parcel continuation. Whether all census/probate/marriage components of this composite candidate belong to him remains correlated. John is omitted, weakening target parentage; mother and Creager identity unstated.

confidence_assessment.assessed_proposition: The reported Abraham Miller, husband of Susanna Creager, may be the Frederick 1820-1830 head and the decedent whose estate entered administration in January 1836
confidence_assessment.rationale: The 1836 Abraham estate, Susan estate and property/sibling records support the cluster. Existing S335 explicitly names the six children/heirs of the Abraham who bought the Grove property in1830; earlier no-explicit-child wording is superseded for that property family. S246 explicitly names Daniel father Abraham. Neither deed names a mother. Correlation of all census/probate components and the exact1765/1835 reported dates remains qualified. S781 relatively solid working identification of the1773 Susanna with Abraham wife is retained; no target John bridge or P066/P067 merge.

evidence.statement: Derivative reconstructions report Abraham Miller married Susanna or Susan Creager about 1792 and give Abraham approximately 1765-1835.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: One page lists only Jacob Thomas Creager Miller while another reports Anna Maria Miller Hedges as a daughter, demonstrating that the reconstructions are incomplete or inconsistent. Neither names John W. A. Miller.

evidence.statement: Original Frederick probate records dated 1836-1839 repeatedly name Susanna Miller and Jacob T. C. Miller as administrators of Abraham Miller, deceased; the administration bond also names Leonard Miller and George Main as obligors.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The matching uncommon Jacob T. C. name independently supports the derivative Abraham-Susanna-Jacob cluster and makes identity with P066 substantially more likely. The originals state administrative roles but not marital or parent-child relationships.

evidence.statement: The 6 February 1836 estate sale repeatedly names Jacob T. C. Miller as a purchaser and also records Susanna or Susan, Daniel, George or George W., and Elizabeth Miller, plus Mary Hedges, buying property from Abraham's estate.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Jacob's co-administration and repeated purchasing, combined with the uncommon full name and the derivative tradition, make the reported son relationship increasingly persuasive. The sale itself never states son, daughter, widow or sibling, so each relationship still requires an explicit or correlated original record.

evidence.statement: Saint John Evangelical Lutheran Church at Creagerstown indexed two children of Abraham Miller and Susanna or Sussanna: Johannes, born 25 August 1795 and christened 6 March 1796, and Anna Maria, born 17 December 1797 and christened 9 April 1798.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: These indexed church entries independently prove that an Abraham-Susanna couple in Creagerstown had children Johannes and Anna Maria. They strongly support the reported Abraham-Susanna family and make the estate-sale Mary Hedges/Anna Maria lead testable. The images are unavailable, and the entries do not by themselves prove that the parents were the 1830 census head or 1836 decedent. The earlier Johannes also complicates any proposal that the same couple later named the target John born about 1824-1825.

evidence.statement: Frederick land indexes record George W. Miller conveying to Jacob T. C. Miller in HS8:473 on 22 April 1839 and Daniel Miller conveying to Jacob T. C. Miller in HS15:269 on 21 January 1842; George W. and Daniel are also recurring names among the 1836 purchasers from Abraham's estate.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The indexed transactions turn two estate-sale names into direct associates of administrator Jacob T. C. Miller and materially strengthen the idea of one cohesive Miller property group. The index and sale do not label kinship, and the original deeds are necessary to distinguish a family transfer from trust, debt, or ordinary sale. Original follow-up29 September2026 is recorded in the newly added deed assessment below.

evidence.statement: Original Frederick records show Jacob T. C. Miller bonded as administrator of Susan Miller on 30 November 1846 and returned her inventory in December. It includes Nance and her child, closely paralleling the Nancy and child in Abraham Miller's 1836 inventory.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The same uncommon administrator and the continuity of a named enslaved mother and child strongly support that this Susan was Abraham's co-administrator and probably the reported Susanna. It also keeps Susan in Frederick County at death, rather than Kentucky. The records do not use the words widow, wife, mother or son, so the exact relationships remain a strongly supported inference rather than direct proof.

evidence.statement: An original 1833 Hunterdon County will names William as a son of John Creger Sr.; an original 1770 recorded will names John as a son of Andries Creeger. Chambers's 1895 genealogy proposes that the 1770 John was the 1833 testator and that his son William, born 6 August 1781, married Ann Nitzer and moved to Ohio.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Each original will directly proves one parent-child pair: Andries to a son John in 1770, and John Creger Sr. to a son William in 1833. The assertion that the two Johns are the same person and that the 1833 William is the Ohio Nitzer husband still rests on the 1895 compilation. Elizabeth Schuyler is not named in either will.

evidence.statement: An 1883 Ohio biography independently reports a New Jersey-born Joseph Creager who came to Ohio about 1820 and whose parents were William and Sarah Nitzer Creager.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Correlates a William/Nitzer New Jersey-to-Ohio cluster with the 1895 book, but 1883 calls the wife Sarah, a separate 1883 biography calls Matilda's mother Catharine Nitzer, and 1895 calls the wife Ann. The original 1850 partition S168 now calls Catharine the widow of W. Creager and assigns shares to Matilda Reddie and Elizabeth Schuyler, placing both married women in this estate family. The original does not say Nitzer, and the wife-given-name conflict remains unresolved.

evidence.statement: A derivative family page reports candidate Susanna Creager born 22 February 1773, baptized 22 March 1773 at Rocky Hill, daughter of George Valentine Creager and Maria Christina; the E&R Archives catalog identifies surviving St. Peters Rocky Hill baptism transcripts covering 1773.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The cited baptism is not yet inspected in the actual church record or historical transcription. The derivative also gives a Kentucky death place contradicted by the 1846 Frederick Susan estate. No evidence reviewed connects the proposed Maryland Valentine/Caspar line to the New Jersey Andries/John/William line.

evidence.statement: Caspar Krueger 1763 Frederick County will directly calls Valentine Krueger his son and names him executor; a published transcript of a 1734 Pennsylvania baptism names George Valentine as a son of Casper Krueger.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The will directly establishes Caspar-to-Valentine parentage. The baptism transcription supports identification with George Valentine born 9 February 1734 in the Oley Mountains, but the original church register has not been inspected. Neither record names the later Susanna as Valentine child or connects Caspar to Andries Creeger of Hunterdon County.

evidence.statement: An original recorded 1770 New Jersey will of Andries Creeger names sons William, John, Peter and Jacob, wife Ann, and daughters Ann, Christian or Christeen, and Elizabeth.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Original Book 15 page 28 confirms the immediate Andries family previously known only through a published abstract. It neither identifies John as the later 1833 Hunterdon testator nor provides a common ancestor with the Maryland Caspar family.

evidence.statement: An 1883 Brown County Ohio biography says Matilda was born in Essex County New Jersey in 1812 to William and Catharine Nitzer and migrated to Ohio about 1817; a later document compilation reports her 1837 marriage as Matilda Cregan.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The 1883 biography is accessed by a transcription that appears to drop Matilda's Creager surname, which the later compilation says is preserved as Cregan in an unexamined original marriage license. The 1850 original partition S168 names Mortimore Reddie and wife Matilda alongside William Skyler and wife Elizabeth among William Creager estate shares; this places the two women in the same heir group. The publications give Nitzer wife given names Ann, Sarah and Catharine; the court record calls the widow Catharine but does not name her maiden name. The migration detail conflicts with Elizabeth's 1900 certificate reporting Ohio birth about January 1816, though her 1850 census S165 reports New Jersey.

evidence.statement: Two later family compilations propose distinct German origins for the earliest Maryland and Hunterdon Creager heads: Caspar from Kleingartach with father Hans Ernst Krieger, and Andries from Heddesdorf with father Johann Wilhelm Krieger.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Neither German original register nor a discriminating migration record has been examined, and each compilation may repeat earlier undocumented research. The different alleged fathers and towns are a testable hypothesis, not proof that the American men were unrelated or that no more remote common ancestor existed.

evidence.statement: The 1850 Miami Township, Clermont County, Ohio census lists a Catharine Creager age 60 born New Jersey in household 1121 with Sarah age 28, Louisa age 26, and Aaron age 24, all Ohio-born.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The original image establishes names, ages, birthplaces and co-residence. The census itself states no household relationships. The 1850 court partition S168 independently identifies a Catharine Creager as widow of deceased W. Creager and names Louisa and Sarah in the heir group; the same-person identification is now strongly supported, although Nitzer is absent from both originals.

evidence.statement: Conrad Creager's 1807 will calls Susannah his daughter; the 1808 will of his widow Mary calls Susanna Buckey her daughter. This strongly distinguishes Conrad's Susanna from the reported Valentine daughter Susanna and Abraham Miller's later Susan.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The two original wills establish Conrad's daughter Susannah and widow Mary's married daughter Susanna Buckey. Their identification as the same daughter is strong. This is evidence against casually merging her with Susan Miller, but an absolute exclusion still needs chronology and marriage identity checks. Neither will connects the New Jersey and Maryland branches.

evidence.statement: An 1834 Clermont marriage return joins Wm Schuyler to Elizabeth Creayer; the 1850 census gives Elizabeth Schuyler age 35 and New Jersey birthplace; an original October 1850 court partition assigns an heir share in deceased W. Creager's land to William Skyler and Elizabeth his wife and dower to widow Catharine Creager.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The partition directly places Elizabeth with husband William Schuyler/Skyler among the named recipients of William Creager land and calls Catharine the widow. With Elizabeth's later certificate naming father Wm Creager, the Ohio father identification is now strong; the court does not explicitly call Elizabeth a daughter or give Catharine's maiden name. The New Jersey birthplace in the 1850 census conflicts with the later death certificate's Ohio birthplace. This evidence does not identify William's New Jersey parents or establish a connection to Maryland Caspar/Valentine.

evidence.statement: A Hunterdon County deed dated 25 April 1817 identifies William Creger and Catharine his wife as Bethlehem Township residents conveying land to Jacob Sigler of Sussex County; the grantor index files the deed in 1820.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: This directly documents a William-Catharine Creger couple in Hunterdon before the Ohio Catharine household in S157 and William estate in S168. The same-person migration trajectory is plausible, especially with Ohio-born Sarah age 28 in 1850, but the deed does not name William parents, cite John Creger, or prove that the couple moved to Ohio. The deed was executed in 1817; 1820 is its index period.

evidence.statement: Original Hunterdon probate packet 4044J for John Creger Sr. includes a wrapper, 1833 inventory, and probate statements; the four consecutive images provide no residence or Ohio identification for son William.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The recorded will S144 expressly names a son William. The separately filmed 4044J packet confirms the same testator and executors but does not supply the needed son residence or Ohio tie. This negative applies only to the four images of packet 4044J; Hunterdon distribution, release, and land series remain unreviewed.

evidence.statement: Official church archive catalogs locate Kleingartach and Schwaigern registers covering the proposed early Caspar Krieger events and a Heddesdorf Reformed register covering proposed Andries antecedents.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The catalogs establish original-register coverage, not individual Krieger entries. Kleingartach book 2 spans 1716-1765; Schwaigern mixed book 2 spans 1700-1789. Archion says Heddesdorf register 213/1, 1673-1747, has no digital scan there. Neither proposed German identity or a common ancestor is established.

evidence.statement: A Hunterdon deed dated 10 May 1815 names William Creger of Bethlehem Township as grantee from Barney Bigler and Catharine his wife of Mansfield Township, Sussex County; the 1817 William-and-Catharine Creger sale cites this purchase.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The 1815 purchase and 1817 sale trace a William Creger landholding in Bethlehem Township and make the two deed appearances the same local land chain. Catharine in the 1815 instrument is Barney Bigler wife; it does not name William wife. The 1817 deed names William wife Catharine. Neither deed identifies William father, later residence, or the deceased Clermont County man. Seller surname has manuscript spelling uncertainty.

evidence.statement: The Hunterdon general estate index 1833 John Creger entry identifies a recorded will and inventory; its facing continuation page has no apparent account, land-division, or release/refunding-bond locator on that row.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The general index is a finding aid and its blank columns constrain only this entry in this index. An unindexed heir receipt or land record might still exist. Handwritten will and inventory volume/folio numerals need closer verification before quoting them.

evidence.statement: Exact microfilm locations for the Rocky Hill original early register and the 1971 fresh translation cover the reported 1773 Susanna baptism; a published translation is also identified in Maryland German Church Records volume 16.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Catalog coverage is not entry verification. The original early register is film 1414858 item 2/DGS 7842502; the translation is item 4 of that film or 845442 item 4/DGS 7578595. Home access to the digitized group is restricted to a FamilySearch Center or affiliate library. Neither baptism nor sponsors were verified from an original.

evidence.statement: A visually reviewed published Harlingen baptism table records child Ante with parents Andiis Krigen and Ante, and witnesses Johannis Crimmelig and Ante Ces, in the 24 February 1751 group.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: This is an earlier church-network lead consistent with the proposed Andries/Ann family, not proof of identity with the 1770 testator. The table does not establish relationships between parents and witnesses. Ces must not silently become Case, and the mother’s purported Fyn/Feyn maiden name is unverified. Full-file text search and selected visual pages did not substantiate the rough pedigree’s 1746 William/1747 John Harlingen dates; other register copies or congregations remain to be checked.

evidence.statement: The Hunterdon historical society inventory locates Jacob and Joseph Nitzer land papers that can test the proposed Catherine maternal family.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Inventory proves a described holding, not the underlying genealogy. Box 3 folder 92 lists Jacob Nitzer deeds in 1786, 1804 and 1806 and Joseph Nitzer in 1816; folder 93 lists Joseph’s 1809 turnpike agreement. Individual documents unexamined; a catalog name match does not establish identity.

evidence.statement: Derivative accounts disagree on the birth/baptism dates of Susanna’s reported brother Thomas and expressly leave Daniel’s placement conjectural.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: S160 assigns Thomas the same 1773 dates as Susanna; S148 instead gives 6 February/28 February 1775. The disagreement concerns what the compilations say, not an established historical birth date. Inspect both 1773 and 1775 register sequences; do not infer twins or adopt a complete sibling set.

evidence.statement: The user-supplied WeRelate Susanna Creager (1) profile explicitly combines the reported 1773 Valentine/Maria Christina daughter with Abraham Miller as husband and Jacob Thomas Creager Miller as child.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: High confidence concerns the page content and identification as the same derivative candidate already studied. The page provides no original citations for the identity bridge; birth/baptism/death and family-page marriage have Citation needed markers. Do not count linked profiles as independent corroboration. Original Frederick Abraham/Susan probate and indexed children support the household but do not establish Susan’s Creager maiden name or Valentine parentage. The page’s 16 July 1846 Kentucky death and alternate before 1869 remain unverified.

evidence.statement: A 2010 Windsor forum compilation transcribes a 3 July 1890 Frederick Daily News obituary identifying Daniel Miller as brother of Jacob T. C. Miller, George W. Miller, Mary M. Hedges and Mrs. Harrison Feete. Its transcribed 1880 Feete household lists Daniel of A. as brother-in-law and Elizabeth A. as Harrison’s wife.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The unusual sibling-name cluster matches names already present in Abraham’s 1836 estate sale (S86) and subsequent Daniel/George W. transactions with Jacob (S89). This is a promising explicit sibling claim, conditional on original newspaper verification. Elizabeth A. Miller Feete is a new collateral candidate for the estate-sale Elizabeth, not an assigned identity. The compiler separately calls Daniel son of Abraham and Susanna Creager, but the quoted obituary does not name either parent and cannot prove Susan’s maiden name or Valentine parentage. The impossible 1906 birth year and apparent stray 1880 census row require originals. No Ohio/NJ Creagar common ancestor or target John relationship established.

evidence.statement: Robert Fry’s 2002 forum reply names Jacob T. C. Miller siblings Mary M. (wife of Shadrach Hedges), Daniel, George W., Elizabeth A. (wife of J. Harrison Feete), and Jane A.; reports Jacob wife Mary Ann Levy, daughter of Jonathan; and proposes a conjectural Abraham Miller/Hutzell ancestry.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The named siblings align with the 1890 obituary transcription (S182) and original estate/land cluster (S86/S89), adding Jane A. and spouse names as useful discriminators. The forum has no original citations, and underlying independence from other reconstructions is unknown. Hutzell ancestry is expressly unconfirmed by the writer and is not adopted as parentage. Parent post S185 expands Mary to Magdalene, whereas S87 indexes Anna Maria; do not merge these names without originals.
