confidence_assessment.assessed_proposition: Baltimore laborer and butcher, father of John W. A. Miller and reported father of Leonard D. Miller.
confidence_assessment.rationale: Emanuel’s 1851 notice identifies his son John W. A. by distinctive initials. John’s known siblings Charlotte and Leonard were in the 1850 Ward 18 household, and Leonard’s 1904 certificate reports Emanuel as his father. The identity with the earlier Frederick records remains open. Leonard’s signed 1864 Middletown statement now supplies specific collateral support for the Frederick hypothesis, while later Baltimore birthplace fields keep the geographic identification unresolved. The Bucher baptism directly names Emanuel and Rebecca as Charlotte’s parents, and the 1850 Baltimore names and middle initial provide a high-confidence link to the later household. The identity with any particular 1840 entry and the 1830 license still require separate correlation.

evidence.statement: Emanuel was 40 and a laborer in Baltimore in 1850 and 52 and a butcher in Baltimore in 1860. Both households include Rebecca and Leonard.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Age estimates are approximate. The census does not state relationships.

evidence.statement: Leonard’s widow supplied the name Emanel Miller for his father and Maryland for his birthplace.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: A late statement consistent with the two earlier households.

evidence.statement: Frederick records give an 1830 license to Emanuel Miller and Rebecca Durbin, a Middletown Emanuel household on Leonard’s 1840 page, and an Emanuel in two probate records.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: These are Frederick leads. Multiple Emanuel candidates and Rebecca’s census age conflict keep the Baltimore identification open.

evidence.statement: Frederick-born Eleanor Miller Spurrier is a strong candidate for the Eleanor enumerated with Emanuel and Rebecca in Baltimore.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Maiden surname, age range, Baltimore residence and 10 Rock Street support correlation. The official death record supplies a Frederick birthplace, but gives no usable parent identification.

evidence.statement: No Emanuel or Emmanuel Miller identified as a primary party in selected Frederick County land index sections, 1822–1851.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Bounded screen of M surname/E given-name entries in both directions. Other spellings or unindexed involvement remain possible.

evidence.statement: Emanuel Miller appears in Frederick County estate sale accounts in 1829, 1831, and 1841. The 1831 account separately names Abraham, Leonard and Eli Miller.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Original names are clear. Repeat associates support continuity in Frederick County, with the identification of the Baltimore Emanuel still open.

evidence.statement: The Baltimore Sun reported an insolvency applicant Emanuel Miller, laborer, in April 1851.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Name, occupation and timing favor the Ward 18 laborer over the Ward 13 clerk. The original petition and address remain outstanding.

evidence.statement: A 1811 Zion Middletown baptism is transcribed as Imaul, with unknown surname and parents.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Possible near-age given-name lead. No Miller attribution can be made.

evidence.statement: A Baltimore directory lists a bricklayer named Emanuel Miller in 1865–66.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The matching Peck household just before Emanuel in 1860 supplies a nearby West Baltimore Street reference. The same name and general neighborhood support further tracing, while the different occupations and lack of a direct address link leave identity open.

evidence.statement: On 28 July 1851 Emanuel Miller of Stockton Alley near Lombard Street identified John W. A. Miller as his son.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The exact name and later sibling and household evidence favor the Ward 18 father. No mother or Frederick residence is stated.

evidence.statement: The Elizabeth Hobbs family occupied the same 1850 Ward 18 dwelling as Emanuel and Rebecca, under a separate family number. A church diary identifies Lorenzo Hobbs Miller near Pratt Street in 1849. The Ward 18 mortality schedule lists two-year-old Lorenzo Hobbs.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The co-residence and diary name are direct readings. Lorenzo’s parentage, Elizabeth’s relationship to Rebecca, and any identification of John A. Hobbs as the later Ohio resident remain hypotheses. The faint month of death appears to read December on the schedule, while its index says August.

evidence.statement: A distinct Emanuel and John Miller, both Pennsylvania-born clerks, appear in Elizabeth Stonebraker’s Ward 13 household in 1850.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The obituary and vault associate Hannah McCauley with a same-name husband and favor the Ward 13 clerk. The indexed Hagerstown baptism is unassigned.

evidence.statement: Frederick administrator John Sifford listed Emanuel Miller in William Perry’s 1836 estate account.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Sifford also appears at the 1831 sale. Continuity between Frederick entries is plausible, with kinship and the Baltimore bridge open.

evidence.statement: The original 1849–50 Matchett directory lists Emanuel Miller, laborer, on Dover Street west of Fremont. It lists Harrison Miller, brakesman, with the same address wording.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Emanuel’s name, occupation and vicinity fit the Ward 18 laborer. Neither entry gives a house number or relationship. John Miller’s separate 15 Dover directory entry has no proven link to either man.

evidence.statement: Delegated review found no new explicit maternal identification for the census children. A1865Rebecca probate notice and1876Jennie death certificate provide separate unassigned leads.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Household association is not biological parentage. Probate decedent and Jennie not identified with this family. InfantKate/Idadeathentries are excluded by age.

evidence.statement: Original1864directory names RebeccaMiller,seamstress,97NorthAmity. Original1865page namesEmanuelbricklayer there;1868/1870originalsnameMrsAnnR.Miller,seamstress,atthataddress.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Highconfidenceinliteralentriesandreviewoutcomes,notP141identity. No attributable parents or deathcertificate recovered. AnnRnotidentifiedasRebecca; no death inferred fromdirectoryomission. Unnamed1808sonofJohnMiller has noEmanuelidentification.

evidence.statement: North Amity follow-up establishes Augustus Hushebeck alone at97 in1880 and directory occupancy by1871, with JohnKlinker also listed97 in1872. The1870Amity neighborhood pp55–57 supplies no identifiedMiller. Rebecca1864/Emanuel1865/AnnR1868–1870 addresscluster remains an identity hypothesis.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Highconfidenceinliteraloriginalreadings and boundedcoverage,not inidentification withP141. NoMillerkinshiptoHushebeck/Magilton/Klinker/Moore; noRebecca=AnnRmerge. AnneMwidEmanuelrear211Hughes favorsseparatenamesakechain butnotdefinitivelyidentified. NoP141deathdate,parents,Abrahamalias ormaternalassignments established.

evidence.statement: In 1840 the original Middletown household of Emanuel Miller has one male each aged 5–9, 10–14 and 30–39, a girl under five and a woman aged 20–29. The facing sheet counts one person in Manufactures and trades.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The male aged 5–9 fits John born about 1832. The older boy is unidentified and was born before the December 1830 license. The adult male's age bracket fits both later Baltimore census ages and still conflicts with the attached 1794 Pennsylvania profile. The census names neither the other household members nor the worker or trade.

evidence.statement: Original Hagerstown registers confirm an unnamed son of Joh. Miller, born 2 October 1808 and baptized 2 January 1809, and a separate Emmanuel, son of John and Elizabeth, born 26 July 1819 and baptized in September 1819.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The 1808 entry leaves the child and maternal personal names blank; no P141 identity is established. The 1819 birth is newly read in the original, not merely inferred from the christening date. It is substantially younger than the P141 census estimates. No Ward 13 identification or kinship is asserted.

evidence.statement: Targeted Frederick indenture and guardian searches, Maryland birth indexes, and selected Lovettsville original-copy baptism pages yielded no attributable new parentage or father-child record. Three new Frederick exact-name court/probate hits remain unread because access is restricted.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Confidence applies to bounded review outcomes, not genealogical absence. All thirty-five early C799-3/4 result excerpts and the C799-5 M index were screened; other guardian and indenture coverage is partial. Lovettsville pp. 94–101 suffer blur and binding loss. Generic 1845 search metadata is not a verified entry date.

evidence.statement: The original Rebecca Miller administration bond of 25 April 1865, C158-7 pp. 272–273, names administrator William Patterson, Daniel R. Wheatley, and another William Patterson signing by mark. The bond is $650.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: No age, address, husband, children or kinship is given. Rebecca remains unassigned. The bond penal sum is not an estate valuation. The original was read online, but its scan was not preserved.

evidence.statement: Verified retrieval routes now include the Bucher original pastoral register, the Frederick 1842–1852 Middletown tax ledger, Washington County childhood indentures, and Baltimore 1848/1851 insolvency and transfer dockets.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: These are precise retrieval targets, not entries demonstrating P141 presence or parents. Bucher requires authorized access; tax contents are unread; specific insolvency packet survival remains unverified. Stonebraker arbitration is retained as namesake context.

evidence.statement: Leonard, identified as John’s brother and reported son of Emanuel, personally stated he was born in Middletown, Maryland. He made that statement in the 1864 signed federal reenlistment.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: 1865 federal forms instead say Baltimore. Evidence strengthens Middletown as the likely locality to investigate but does not identify the 1840 head as the same man, establish John’s birth there, or name Emanuel’s parents.

evidence.statement: A Washington County estate dividend names Emanl Miller by February 1833, repeated in the third Slifer account.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: High confidence in the creditor entry; his identity, residence and kinship remain unassigned. The 1819 namesake’s age makes the identification doubtful but does not establish P141 as the creditor.

evidence.statement: Leonard’s 1904 obituary records unnamed Carroll County relatives. The county had a Middletown around Bark Hill, near Uniontown.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The obituary leaves the relatives’ identities and side of the family open. The 1904 Spurrier visit points to a younger namesake and supplies no Emanuel relationship. The Frederick original parentage and tax leads remain unresolved.

evidence.statement: Carroll County’s original 1868 and 1871 marriage records and the 1850/1870 censuses identify Margaret E. Miller Pfeiffer and Harriet A. Miller in the Gamber collateral research.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The combined records strongly favor Harriet as Clinton Pfeiffer’s aunt and Thomas J. as his uncle by marriage. The Gamber reports do not name a relative of Emanuel or Edward’s widow Ella.

evidence.statement: The Zion typescript names Michael Hump ? and wife as sponsors of Imaul in 1811. An approximately contemporaneous Suman baptism has a similarly spelled sponsor, and the Frederick indexes document the 1803 Michael Humbert–Mary Bussard license. The Samuel Buzzard estate abstract links Mary Humbert and Anna Suman as sisters.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The combined records provide a candidate sponsor household, with no established link to Emanuel Miller. The German entry and the original estate pages remain unread. The separate Michal Humbert aged 17 in 1814 could not have been the 1803 groom if his age was accurate.

evidence.statement: The Frederick bride index contains three Rebecca Durbin license entries, two earlier than the 1830 Emanuel Miller entry.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Applies to the names and issuance dates only. No identification of one woman across entries, connection to Baltimore Rebecca, or officiant established.

evidence.statement: The reviewed Apple register, January 1831 Frederick Herald and selected Frederick Orphans Bound pages yielded no attributable target-family entry.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Applies only to the defined ranges. The Apple register does include delayed baptisms; the result does not exhaust Middletown churches or prove a birthplace.

evidence.statement: The Magruder estate account groups Titlow, Buzzard and Humbert names in 1831 witness fee entries. The Durbin estate docket and bond identify Nicholas as executor, with no Rebecca Lindsay payment or marriage information.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The records show a collateral association and an executor appointment, not a tie to Emanuel. An adjacent 1832 account belongs to William Duvall.

evidence.statement: The Maryland State Archives reproduction log locates June 1830 and March 1831 licenses in Book 3 on p. 128 and pp. 134–135, respectively.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The suggested lookup range is inferred from nearby chronological entries. The target entry is not in the reproduction log and its exact page and contents are unverified.

evidence.statement: The 1825 Middletown fire-company act names Adam Herring and Michael Beckenbaugh together. Van Swearingen appears on Emanuel's page in the Herring sale and on his 1840 Middletown census sheet, which also lists Henry Herring and the Rev. J. C. Bucher.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The place and associates favor continuity for the Frederick Emanuel. The records do not state a family relationship among the sale buyers or establish the Baltimore identity.

evidence.statement: The 21 April 1813 Frederick license was issued to Edward Fowler and Rebecca Durbin. An Edward Fowler named his wife Rebecca in his 1863 Carroll County will.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The couple in 1863 is a strong candidate for the 1813 pair. The will supplies no maiden name. This evidence does not identify the 1830 bride.

evidence.statement: The Western Maryland Genealogy volume 3 name index lists Charlotte, Emanuel and Rebecca Miller on journal p. 163 of Margaret E. Myers’s Bucher register transcription.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The three names match the 1850 Baltimore household cluster and identify a specific page to read. The index gives neither event roles nor dates. The historical entry and identification of its people remain unverified.

evidence.statement: The two FamilySearch hits are reciprocal Frederick County marriage license index cards for Emmanuel Miller and Rebecca Durbin dated 29 December 1830. Four user photos show two views of each card.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The cards agree with the date-of-issuance entries in the county bride and groom indexes (S2196). The “m.” abbreviation supplies no separate ceremony date. No parents, ages, officiant, witnesses, or volume/page citation are visible on the cards. The Book 3 entry remains unread, and neither the bride’s identity in Baltimore nor John W. A. Miller’s maternity is established. The photos do not show which ARK belongs to each card.

evidence.statement: Frederick County issued a license to Margaret Durbin and David Lindsey on 30 November 1805. William Durbin’s 1820 will gives his granddaughter Rebecca Lindsey $500 payable at age 18.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The license and the granddaughter are directly attested. Margaret and David’s parentage of Rebecca is a compiled hypothesis. No original record connects the granddaughter to the 1830 bride, and the proposed earlier birth conflicts with later age reports.

evidence.statement: The six indexed 1830 Frederick County Durbin heads were in District 7. Mary Sullivan appears directly after William Durbin, and her will names William, his wife Elizabeth and several Durbin beneficiaries.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: This supports tracing the Westminster and New Windsor area families. The enumeration does not name William’s household members. The will’s selective bequests give no link to the 1830 bride.

evidence.statement: William Durbin’s granddaughter Rebecca Lindsey was licensed to Isaac Pouder on 6 August 1827. Their receipt of 1 December 1828 describes them as husband and wife and acknowledges $500 from Nicholas Durbin.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The receipt establishes her married name by December 1828. It does not name her parents. Isaac’s reported divorce petition has no verified outcome (S2442), and no record connects Rebecca Pouder to the 1830 Miller license.

evidence.statement: Benjamin Durbin’s 1813 will names daughters Rebecca, Comfort and Catharine. Catharine’s 1849 will names her sisters Comfort Durbin and Rebecca Fowler.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The sister names and Edward Fowler license and probate strongly identify Benjamin’s Rebecca with the Fowler family. This supports setting that candidate aside for Emanuel’s 1830 bride. It establishes no relationship to Emanuel.

evidence.statement: The Frederick groom James Durbin was a son of Thomas W. Durbin of Carroll County. A Seneca County mortgage names the same Maryland creditor and note as Thomas Wills’s bequest to James. Samuel R. Durbin’s 1861 final account identifies eight siblings, including James, Charity Hyter, Sarah Harrison and Thomas W. Durbin.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Neither the 1841 named bequests nor the 1861 intestate sibling distribution lists Rebecca. This weighs against identifying Emanuel Miller’s bride as James’s surviving sister. A more distant Durbin relationship remains open. S2462 is a shared page reference only.

evidence.statement: Thomas W. Durbin’s 1859 final estate account calls James his son. Its full distribution allocates nine children’s shares among eight recipients. The widow Sarah survived Thomas by about six weeks.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The complete allocation and Samuel’s later sibling distribution both weigh against Rebecca being a surviving sister. The 1888 William biography gives Sarah’s maiden surname McKnight and a larger family count. James’s mother and the extra names or children need independent verification.

evidence.statement: In 1820 a Thomas W. Durbin witnessed and proved William Durbin’s Frederick County will. The will describes land by a boundary with Thomas Wills. In the bulletin index the Rebecca entry likely refers to the 1801 Dell bride.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Name, place and the Wills association support identifying the witness as James’s father. The will gives no relationship to William. The Dell reading is inferred from the index and license. Bulletin p. 74 remains unread.

evidence.statement: Charity Durbin’s 1844 will expressly identifies Thomas W. Durbin as her son. Thomas’s final account calls James Durbin his son. Charity is James’s paternal grandmother.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The 1820 will, 1829 bank act and 1840 census strongly support identifying her with William Durbin’s sister. Thomas Wills’s paternity and Rebecca’s relationship remain unproved.

evidence.statement: Nicholas Durbin’s 1865 final account identifies Susan Eby and Mary Nicodemus as daughters and Andrew Reese Durbin as son. The three divide the full distributable balance.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The distribution agrees with the earlier Reese chancery abstract. It weighs against Rebecca Miller being Nicholas and Catharine’s daughter and links the bulletin’s Nicodemus names to this branch. The bulletin page remains unread.

evidence.statement: The printed Durbin Dictionary p. 48 cites a Kentucky Historical Society Durbin Family Folder, copied by Charles Dochterman, for the 29 December 1830 Emanuel Miller and Rebecca Durbin entry.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Confidence refers to what the printed page says. The cited folder remains unread. The matching FamilySearch profile and reviewed Ancestry tree supply no parents.

evidence.statement: Bucher baptized Charlotte on 5 April 1838 and names Emanuel and Rebecca Miller as her parents. The sponsor is Grandmother Charlotte Miller.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The 1850 Baltimore household includes Charlotte P., age 13, with Emanuel and Rebecca Miller (S2192). Her middle initial and later Baltimore records support a high-confidence identification. A March 1838 birth would make her 12 at the 1850 enumeration. Rebecca’s maiden name and identity with the 1830 Durbin bride remain open. The sponsor’s Miller surname favors investigating her as Emanuel’s mother. The register does not specify the parental side. Charlotte Main/Mohn (P012), wife of Leonard Miller, is a distinct candidate for the sponsor based on name, age and locality. Leonard’s paternity is unproved.

evidence.statement: The likely 1810 Middletown L. Miller household has one boy under ten. Leonard’s named households have one boy 10–15 in 1820 and one man 20–29 in 1830.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The sequence fits a birth about 1808–1810 if the three people counted were the same. Abraham’s 1830 household also had age-compatible men. No reviewed record names Emanuel as Leonard or Charlotte Main’s son. The possibility that Emanuel was born in 1811 gives a different census expectation.

relationships.basis: S2481 calls Charlotte Miller the grandmother of Emanuel and Rebecca’s daughter. Her Miller surname favors the paternal hypothesis, while the parental side is unstated.

Leonard’s 1820 and 1830 household age brackets can fit Emanuel. The two men appear separately in the 1831 Herring sale and the 1840 Middletown census. The records establish local association and leave paternity open.

The 1838 baptism names Grandmother Charlotte Miller. George Main’s estate names his daughter Charlotte as Leonard Miller’s wife. Charlotte Main is a candidate for the sponsor. The baptism leaves the sponsor’s identity and side of the family open.

conflicts_and_cautions: The Baltimore Rebecca would have been about ten at the 1830 license if the reported ages are accurate.
The 1870 Easton, Talbot County family headed by Emanuel Miller, 63, is a namesake group (S2229). Keep its children and unverified Talbot death separate.
The June 1860 heir deed omits Emanuel from the named children of the 1836 Frederick Abraham. The 1831 sale gives separately named Emanuel and Abraham purchases.
The 1819 Hagerstown baptism index for a son of John and Elizabeth Miller is unassigned. The 1850 Baltimore Ward 13 clerk is demonstrably a separate census subject from this man.

The corrected 1840 Middletown male age 30–39 fits the Baltimore ages of 40 in 1850 and 52 in 1860. It conflicts with the 1794 birth displayed on the FamilySearch profile 267B-1J2 to which the source is attached. The displayed Andre Miller/Mary Magdalena Rudisill parents have no documented link to P141.

The original Hagerstown 1808 son has no given name. The original gives the named Emmanuel a birth date of 26 July 1819, rather than merely a christening-year inference. Neither establishes P141 parents.
Leonard’s military papers disagree on Middletown versus Baltimore. The Washington County Slifer creditor is unassigned; the 1865 April Rebecca is also unassigned.
The signed military form supplies no county. Frederick County is the leading Middletown hypothesis, but Baltimore County ED 6 also had a historical Middletown (S2333).
unresolved_questions: Was the 1840 Middletown head the Baltimore butcher? Who were Emanuel’s parents, spouse or spouses, and children?
Did the Elizabeth Hobbs household in dwelling 966 or Lorenzo Hobbs Miller belong to Emanuel and Rebecca’s family network?
What was Thomas W. Durbin’s relationship to the William whose 1820 will he likely witnessed, and can a collateral Durbin branch identify Emanuel’s 1830 bride?
Was Grandmother Charlotte Miller Emanuel’s mother, and was she Charlotte Main/Mohn (P012)?
next_research_actions: Trace Grandmother Charlotte Miller from the 1838 Bucher baptism. Compare Charlotte Main/Mohn and Leonard Miller with the original 1820 and later sponsor records and seek an explicit parent-child or estate/heir record linking Emanuel to the sponsor. Check the maternal alternative.

incoming.basis: S2249 is Emanuel’s own 1851 statement naming John W. A. Miller as his son. Distinctive initials, West Baltimore context, and the 1874 sibling report support the identification.
S2193 reports Emanel Miller as his father, corroborated by the S2192 and S2121 households. S2249 independently identifies Emanuel as the father of Leonard’s known brother John.
S2481 directly names Emanuel Miller as the father. S2192 and Charlotte’s later Baltimore records support the identification.

P142.research_role: Frederick-born wife of Edward Spurrier and possible member of Emanuel Miller’s Baltimore family.

confidence_assessment.assessed_proposition: Ella Spurrier and the bride Elanor Miller identify one woman, plausibly the Elenora J. of Emanuel’s Baltimore household.
confidence_assessment.rationale: Original marriage, 1880 census, death notice and death certificate agree. Ella occupied 10 Rock Street, where Charlotte’s funeral was later held.

evidence.statement: Elanor Miller married Edward Spurrier on 13 November 1863 in Baltimore. Both were of Baltimore.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The officiant is Rev. Mr. Hamilton. The notice does not identify parents or an exact venue.

evidence.statement: Ella Spurrier and daughters Anna and Ella lived at 10 Rock Street in 1880. Charlotte McLaughlin’s 1883 funeral was from the same dwelling address.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The address connection is direct. Its meaning for kinship is inferred.

evidence.statement: Ella, widow of Edward, died 18 September 1917 at 1201 West Lexington Street, age 74, and was buried at Loudon Park.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Birthplace is reported as Frederick, Maryland. Father unknown. The mother field repeats the decedent’s maiden name. Birth year 1843 is approximate.

evidence.statement: Possible identity with Elenora J., 10 in 1850 and Ellenor, 19 in 1860, in Emanuel and Rebecca’s Baltimore household.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: Census ages and shared address with the McLaughlin family support correlation. The unsourced parent assertion in a member tree remains a lead.

evidence.statement: Original1863marriage notice reread confirms13November, not the11November in a derivative transcript. Additional21September1917funeral notice names no parents or new relatives.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The marriage date is confirmed; connection to Emanuel/Rebecca remains an indirect candidate correlation.

evidence.statement: The 12 November 1863 Baltimore license gives Ella Miller and Edward Spurrier, with Hamilton as minister. The 1899 notice confirms Ella as Edward’s wife.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The 13 November wedding notice gives Elanor. The 1904 visitor called Ella Spurrier strongly correlates to Margaret E. Pfeiffer, wife of James W. Spurrier. No record here names a parent for Edward’s wife.

evidence.statement: Carroll County’s original 1868 and 1871 marriage records and the 1850/1870 censuses identify Margaret E. Miller Pfeiffer and Harriet A. Miller in the Gamber collateral research.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The combined records strongly favor Harriet as Clinton Pfeiffer’s aunt and Thomas J. as his uncle by marriage. The Gamber reports do not name a relative of Emanuel or Edward’s widow Ella.

conflicts_and_cautions: Approximate birth year 1840–1841 from the candidate censuses versus 1843 in D8625. The middle name Julian appears in a member tree.
unresolved_questions: Can a primary record link Eleanor to Emanuel and Rebecca and identify her precise Frederick birthplace?
next_research_actions: Check Franklin Street Methodist Episcopal class rolls 1860–1875 and surviving marriage materials for Rev. William Hamilton. Search Frederick records for an Eleanor Miller born around 1840–1843.

P143.research_role: Son of Irvin McLaughlin named in probate and likely the Charles in Irvin and Charlotte’s census household.

confidence_assessment.assessed_proposition: Charles was Irvin’s son. His mother’s identity remains open.
confidence_assessment.rationale: The 1890 account names Charles as son and only heir. The 1870 household and the 10 Rock Street directory and funeral address correlate Charles L. with Irvin and Charlotte. Later census and obituaries match by address, occupation and family.

evidence.statement: The 1870 census shows Charles L., 12, in the constable’s household with Charlotte P. Directory text places Charles L. at 10 Rock Street, from which Charlotte’s funeral was held in 1883.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The census does not state relationships. Adult identity is correlated by the address and name.

evidence.statement: On 31 May 1890 the administrator identified Charles as Irvin’s son and only heir, and recorded payment of $259.96.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The record gives no mother’s name.

evidence.statement: Censused as an electrician in 1920 at 2017 West Mulberry with Ella and Milton. The same address appears in the 1923 notice for Ella and the 1930 obituary for Charles.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The obituary states age 70 and five surviving sons. The 1930 certificate is a separate retrieval target.

relationships.basis: S2222 directly identifies Charles as Irvin’s son. S1934 and the 10 Rock Street evidence identify the family.

conflicts_and_cautions: Exclude the teenage Charles Irwin, son of Joseph and Rebecca, died 1875 (S2215–S2216).
The reported 1860 and 1870 ages place birth before the 1859 marriage, and the 1930 obituary implies a later birth around 1859–1860.
unresolved_questions: What do original birth, baptism or death records report for his birth date and mother?
next_research_actions: Read Baltimore death certificate E56619, CM1132-177, and the Mount Olivet Cemetery caretaker entry. Compare the 1890 probate heir release.

P144.research_role: Mother of Charlotte as named in Bucher’s 1838 baptism register, correlated with the Rebecca in Emanuel Miller’s 1850 Baltimore household.

confidence_assessment.assessed_proposition: Rebecca Miller is named as Charlotte’s mother in 1838 and is strongly identified with Rebecca in the Baltimore household.
confidence_assessment.rationale: The 1850 Baltimore household includes Charlotte P., age 13, with Emanuel and Rebecca Miller (S2192). Her middle initial and later Baltimore records support a high-confidence identification. A March 1838 birth would make her 12 at the 1850 enumeration. Rebecca’s maiden name and identity with the 1830 Durbin bride remain open.

evidence.statement: Bucher’s 1838 baptism names Rebecca and Emanuel Miller as Charlotte’s parents.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The row reads Charlotte Parmelia (middle-name spelling provisionally read), parents Emanuel and Rebecca Miller, sponsor Grandmother Charlotte Miller. The baptism column gives 5 April in the 1838 sequence. The far-right birth column appears to give 7 March 1838. The entry supplies no maiden name for Rebecca, no maiden name or parental side for the sponsor, and no verified ceremony location. The 1850 Baltimore household includes Charlotte P., age 13, with Emanuel and Rebecca Miller (S2192). Her middle initial and later Baltimore records support a high-confidence identification. A March 1838 birth would make her 12 at the 1850 enumeration. Rebecca’s maiden name and identity with the 1830 Durbin bride remain open.

evidence.statement: Frederick County issued a marriage license to Emanuel Miller and Rebecca Durbin on 29 December 1830.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The license establishes the bride’s name. Correlating her with Charlotte’s mother remains a separate question, with a census-age discrepancy.

conflicts_and_cautions: The baptism supplies no maiden name. The 1850 and 1860 census ages would place Baltimore Rebecca at about ten in December 1830 if accurate.
The baptism establishes Charlotte’s recorded maternity. The maternity of John W. A., Leonard D., and other children requires separate evidence.
unresolved_questions: Was Charlotte’s mother the Rebecca Durbin licensed to Emanuel Miller on 29 December 1830? Who were her parents?
next_research_actions: Obtain the 1830 license entry in Maryland State Archives C825-3. Compare the original Bucher baptism and nearby entries with documents that name Rebecca’s maiden name or relatives.

incoming.basis: S2481 directly names Rebecca Miller as the mother. Her maiden name remains unresolved.

evidence.statement: The sponsor column for the 5 April 1838 baptism names Grandmother Charlotte Miller.
evidence.interpretation_and_limitations: The sponsor’s Miller surname favors investigating her as Emanuel’s mother. The register does not specify the parental side. Charlotte Main/Mohn (P012), wife of Leonard Miller, is a distinct candidate for the sponsor based on name, age and locality. Leonard’s paternity is unproved.

conflicts_and_cautions: Retain this sponsor separately from the baptized child and from Charlotte Main/Mohn (P012).
unresolved_questions: Was the sponsor Emanuel’s mother or Rebecca’s mother? Was she Charlotte Main/Mohn, or the Charlotte Miller who sponsored Emeline Eliza Hergesheimer in 1820?
next_research_actions: Compare S2481 with the 1820 baptism in S279 and the documented Middletown records for P012. Seek a probate, deed, or church record explicitly linking Emanuel or Rebecca to this sponsor.

S110.title: James M. Miller et al. v. John Bryant Sr. and James Bryant, Adair Circuit Court equity case
S110.record_locator: Adair Circuit Court, equity; petition filed 8 January 1858; 102-page digitized case file; petition at PDF pp. 3-6; public access page https://kygenweb.net/adair/Court_Records/miller-equity.html
S110.review_status:
Cover and petition reviewed 20 September 2026. On 2 October all 102 pages screened at contact-sheet resolution; selected pages enlarged, as recorded in E089. Not fully transcribed. Expanded review: John Bryant’s answer, PDF pp. 31–33, acknowledges Samuel’s death in Adair, his children/heirs and deceased widow Huldah, while contesting acreage and alleging cancelled or settled contracts. The certified May Term 1863 judgment, pp. 93–94, awards the south-side Russell Creek tract of 30 or 40 acres. The survey conducted 21 October and reported 22 October 1863, p. 98, measures 37¼ acres. Final judgment p. 100 confirms the survey and orders possession by 1 January 1864. The 150 acres was a disputed pleaded claim, not the final award. Proposed transfers in draft pp. 95–96 are crossed out, not established conveyances. Alexander Bryant p. 69 supposes a return to Pulaski in 1846, versus the petition’s 1847/48. No Samuel parents or birthplace found in the selected detailed review. Enlarged petition PDFpp3–4 rechecked: p4 explicitly Huldah(motherofPlffs), correcting previous not-express-maternity assessment. p3 initial deathyear appears184 with finaldigit omitted/unclear; p4 clearly fall1844 move and Christmasthereafter death, supporting court chronology1844. New1845Samuel/Huldah deeds conflict; deathyear unresolved. OriginalPDF unchanged.

3 October2026 expanded manual original-image review of PDFpp43–90, not an exhaustive diplomatic transcription. Source PDF E089/download.pdf remains unchanged and is not duplicated. PDFpp43–49 identify Elijah Leach (NOT the examiner JohnS.Browning): Leach says the widow selected him to hold the bond when returning from Samuel's burial; he retained it until she called for it. He could not read and heard others read it; he did not personally know the original purchase. PDFp50 Francis McElroy says the widow brought him a title bond after Samuel's death; he kept it about six months and returned it to her; he personally read it, recalling150acres south of Russell Creek. No fixed custody sequence between Leach and McElroy established. PDFpp51–57 Henry Light says he was an adjoining resident, read the original150-acre bond, and knew of a later50-acre arrangement without a writing known to him. PDFpp53–54 Light says John Bryant told him he obtained the bond from the widow in exchange for a horse and put it in the fire; Light did not witness the burning. The account of the Miller boys being frightened away by war talk and going to Pulaski is likewise Light's report of Bryant's statements, not proof of any pre-Kentucky residence. These are the Bryant–Samuel Adair contracts, NOT the separate Light→Samuel→Graves Pulaski assignment.

PDFpp63–73 Alexander Bryant deposition19November1859: p63 says acquaintance began about six weeks before Samuel died, knew children but could not name them; p64 says Samuel and John Bryant came to Alexander Bryant at his schoolhouse, where Alexander says he was teaching school, to discuss revised boundaries. Corrected 3 October 2026: the first-person teacher is the witness Alexander, not Samuel. p65 recalls Samuel saying he was sickly and the smaller tract was sufficient; p67 cannot say whether adult children moved to Pulaski before their mother; p68 thinks all under21 without certainty; p69 supposes return1846. p70 says only the first trade had writing as far as he knew, and cannot give precise interval before schoolhouse discussion. This places Samuel at a meeting at Alexander Bryant’s schoolhouse; it does not establish Samuel as a teacher and supplies no school name, parents, birthplace, exact age or prior Virginia residence. The100-acre original acreage remembered here conflicts with Leach/McElroy/Light150: preserve both and the later30–40/37.25-acre award, not select a universal acreage.

PDFpp75–84 DanielB.Bryant and JosephBryant depositions November1860: p76 says widow and all children except Jacob and John consented to a horse/move-to-Pulaski/notes settlement, with John perhaps present; p77 estimates Jacob~21,James23or24,John~20,Nancy~18 and others younger at Samuel's death, aboutsixmonths on land thenfamily six/eightmonths more. These are fallible estimates, inconsistent with some1840/1889 age implications; no new dates or identities fixed. p79 Daniel expressly says he is John Bryant's son. p83 Joseph says he never saw writings, only Samuel told him there was a first one. PDFpp85–90 affidavit and laterWilliamBryant/ThomasCorvin depositions contain contract/property testimony; no earlier-origin bridge identified. William's pp87–88 conversation with Samuel shortly before death repeats planned cancellation and intended deed for a smaller south-side tract. All reviewed48pages yielded no named Samuel parents, Huldah maiden name, pre-Kentucky locality, or copy of the missing Pulaski assignment. Negative limited to this selected detailed page range; remaining earlier pages have prior contact-sheet/selected review, not fully transcribed. Death-year contradiction between court1844 narrative and1845Samuel/Huldah deeds remains unresolved.

# Original deed abstract, reviewed 2 October 2026

16 August 1848, John, James, Henry, Nancy (now Nancy Alexander) and William Light, heirs of deceased John Light, convey two adjoining 50-acre tracts to John Colyer senior for $400. Parties described collectively as of Pulaski and Adair counties; individual residences are not assigned.

Pulaski deed book 13, pp.441–442; DGS008193855 image232/384. Original opening reads payment to Hiram Graves, who was assignee of “Saml Miller”, who was assignee of John Light, “the title now being in us”. Saml is the original abbreviation; Samuel is its usual expansion. This is a recorded copy, not the parties' autograph instrument.

First tract: Pitmans Creek, Blaze Hollow; John Hunt's last corner and line, Burks conditional line, James Christy's old corner, Jesse Richardson/Hiram Hughs conditional line. Second tract: southeast of the first, Ferrells Hollow, Burks former survey and Richardson line. Several bearings/distances are faint; no certified survey or modern geolocation made. Keep this estate's 100 acres separate from Samuel's 100-acre Buck Creek Meace purchase.

Copy signatures/acknowledgment include John/Permelia, Henry/Nancy, James/[Nancy Jane in acknowledgment], Cyrenius/Nancy Alexander, William Light. Russell County acknowledgment appears [26?] August 1848, by George Bryan deputy for William S. Patterson; day overwritten/uncertain. Pulaski recording certificate and William Light additional acknowledgment: 20 May 1850. AI text misreads dates and clerk name; use image.

Target Samuel identity probable, supported by Light–Miller–Graves and Blaze Hollow continuity with 1845 eight-acre transactions, but wife absent and original assignment date absent. Not a proof of Samuel's parents, Virginia residence, 1837 nineteen-acre acquisition, ownership of all 100 acres, or survival to 1848. Both 50-acre surveys need prior-title recovery. Original assignment itself not recovered.

E087.transcription:
E087 - Handwritten Miller family tradition account

Diplomatic transcription prepared 19 September 2026 from the five-page image-only PDF supplied as nellie_alt_miller.pdf. Original spelling, capitalization, and punctuation are retained as closely as practical. Line wrapping is normalized into paragraphs. Words supplied or uncertain are enclosed in square brackets. Struck-out wording is omitted when a clear replacement is present. The scan remains authoritative.

PDF PAGE 1 (unnumbered manuscript page)

John William Alexander Miller

The Miller family history begins with John Wm A. the son of Abraham Miller. John was born about 1825 in Washington D. C. Near 1849-50 he married Anna Elizabeth Blackstone, who was born in Devonshire England. She had lived in a place of the same name as that of her father. If true such a circumstance would ordinarily indicate she came of a more or less landed gentry.

So far the family story poses a mystery unsolvable. As searching has been done in all areas without success.

How or where did John meet a lady of her class and who was disowned for marrying him. It is interesting to speculate on the circumstances of the match. But to find the facts requires a great deal more research.

To John and Anna Elizabeth was born a son named -

John Thomas Miller

Note

Since the above was written I have learned John W. A. Miller was born in Germany. Which clears up the problem of his marriage to Anna Elizabeth Blackstone. We can assume they were married in England. And now the search goes to there.

PDF PAGE 2 (manuscript page 2)

Son George also stated John went to Baltimore and worked as an apprentice under John Wm. Bruce. Which would indicate some friendly connection between the Miller and Bruce families.

John Wm Bruce worked for the Baltimore and Ohio railroad in their shops, as did as many as four or five of his sons through the years. While John Thomas was learning blacksmithing he lived with the Bruces. But apparently he did not follow the Bruces to Piedmont W. Va. when John Bruce was transferred to superintend the big Baltimore and Ohio shop there. No one of the Bruce family ever mentioned John Miller.

But in 1872 he went to Westernport, just across the river from Piedmont W. Va., to marry Annah Bruce. The marriage license dated 13, September 1872 shows Johns age as twenty and his residence as Baltimore Md. and painter as his occupation. Anna is noted as W. Anna Bruce age seventeen. She never used her name Williamannah. Who could blame her? What a terrible name to give a little girl. I think just because she was the seventh daughter and daddy thought he would never have another son he could name William, then he did have one right after Anna. He should have been more patient.

But back to John T. We wonder if he did learn to be a blacksmith. For painter fits better with the story of his being a carriage painter. And that he also made calling cards. And we know how they were so beautifully done by hand, and would be of the same fine painstaking form of art.

Johns and Annahs family soon began to arrive, and grow.

PDF PAGE 3 (newspaper clipping)

Funeral To Be Held Wednesday For J. T. Miller

Funeral services will be held this afternoon at 2:30 from the chapel of the Baldwin Park Funeral Home for John Thomas Miller, 87, of 1425 E. Valley boulevard, El Monte, who passed away November 20.

Mr. Miller, who was born April 17, 1851, at Washington D. C., had been a resident of El Monte three years and of the state 12 years.

The deceased a widower, is survived by three sons, Asa Miller, 217 Bogart street, John R. Miller, 134 N. Center street, Baldwin Park, and George Miller of St. Louis; and two daughters, Mrs. Emma Prosser and Mrs. Lula Lutten, both of 1425 E. Valley, El Monte.

Burial will be in the Rose Hills cemetery.

PDF PAGE 4 (manuscript page 3)

You can follow that growth on the family record sheet. She was such a little thing to have so many children. We know she was a small and attractive young girl.

The family started out with Charles Asa, as you can see, who was born in Westernport Md. Also the sister who followed him, the next little girl [Erma?] born in Piedmont W. Va., and both died in their infancy.

What a terrible blow to the young parents. Emma and Oliver were, also born in W. Va., William in Minnesota, John in Joliet Ill. also George, and Lula in E. St. Louis Ill.

Life was not easy for the little mother Annah. For John was a rover from his early years. The first long trip was made to Cedar Rapids Iowa when Oliver was only seven months old because he had a job there. They were a much traveled family before they finally landed in E. St. Louis. Johns itchy feet had kept them moving ever farther west. No wonder Charles Asa said the main thing he remembered was "moving."

The families life seemed settled down in St Louis. And the family grew up and some were married and had children. Son Olivers daughter told me the only thing she remembers about the family in St Louis was that her grandparents lived on a farm. That was just surprising! Nomads dont farm, they just move on to greener pastures. They really needed time to rest I guess.

But farm they did, or at least lived on one. For the grand daughter recalls all of the apples she ate there. And they must have raised a lot of carrots for I recall dad Asa saying he never wanted to eat another carrot, he got sick of them.

While the Millers lived in St. Louis many members of Annahs

PDF PAGE 5 (manuscript page 4)

Bruce family came to visit them, as many of them had passes for railroad travel and others were financially able to afford it, many made trips out to see them. This of course would have made Annah very happy. For she was so isolated from all of her fathers family.

It is not possible to say how long the family lived in St. Louis. But several of the family were married there and had there children born there. Son George was the only one of the family who never came west. He said the Bruces were still visiting in St Louis as late as 1905 as there were out to see the Worlds Fair there.

Some time along the way the family resided in Clifton, and there is no record of when they came to Calif. to live. Where six of them later died, correction, seven of the family died in California.

Not enough is known of Johns and Annahs family to give more than a few biographical notes.

Charles Asa was a plumbing and heating contractor. Olivers daughter said her father was a coal and ice dealer. He had the largest family, eight children. Asa had seven, but raised five. George had three, he was a city man, urbane, pleasant and self-assured. John was an inventor, a builder and full of ideas. He invented the home water heater. He served in World War I and fought in France. He and wife May had no children, neither did Erma, nor Wallace who married late and died very soon after. Lula had two children.

John and Annah did well as the progenitors and founders of the Miller clan and a family to be proud of who in turn have followed in their footsteps.

Note - John T. Miller came to Cal. in 1938

CORRECTION, 3 October 2026: PDF p. 64 is Alexander Bryant speaking in the first person: "I was called on at my school house where I was teaching school". Samuel Miller and John Bryant visited him there. The teacher is Alexander Bryant, not Samuel. The passage supplies no schoolhouse name and does not establish a teaching occupation for Samuel. Expanded review: John Bryant’s answer, PDF pp. 31–33, acknowledges Samuel’s death in Adair, his children/heirs and deceased widow Huldah, while contesting acreage and alleging cancelled or settled contracts. The certified May Term 1863 judgment, pp. 93–94, awards the south-side Russell Creek tract of 30 or 40 acres. The survey conducted 21 October and reported 22 October 1863, p. 98, measures 37¼ acres. Final judgment p. 100 confirms the survey and orders possession by 1 January 1864. The 150 acres was a disputed pleaded claim, not the final award. Proposed transfers in draft pp. 95–96 are crossed out, not established conveyances. Alexander Bryant p. 69 supposes a return to Pulaski in 1846, versus the petition’s 1847/48. No Samuel parents or birthplace found in the selected detailed review.

Explicitly calls Eliza Ann a child and heir of deceased Robert B. Windsor, who left three children and a widow. The property is Jefferson (formerly New Town Trap), lot51, 82 feet wide by 284 feet deep, previously conveyed by Christian Tabler and Sarah his wife to Robert B. Windsor, HS16:255, 28 March1842. After dower, debts and expenses, the proceeds of her portion are to be paid to Eliza Ann. Adjacent widow Elizabeth Windsor dower release also refers to this lot. This is Windsor inheritance, not Daniel’s Abraham-derived Middletown share. Wife, suffix and associates strengthen correlation with the reported1890 Daniel; this deed names no parent of Daniel, sibling, John or Susanna.

# Original deed abstract, reviewed 2 October 2026

16 August 1848, John, James, Henry, Nancy (now Nancy Alexander) and William Light, heirs of deceased John Light, convey two adjoining 50-acre tracts to John Colyer senior for $400. Parties described collectively as of Pulaski and Adair counties; individual residences are not assigned.

Pulaski deed book 13, pp.441–442; DGS008193855 image232/384. Original opening reads payment to Hiram Graves, who was assignee of “Saml Miller”, who was assignee of John Light, “the title now being in us”. Saml is the original abbreviation; Samuel is its usual expansion. This is a recorded copy, not the parties' autograph instrument.

First tract: Pitmans Creek, Blaze Hollow; John Hunt's last corner and line, Burks conditional line, James Christy's old corner, Jesse Richardson/Hiram Hughs conditional line. Second tract: southeast of the first, Ferrells Hollow, Burks former survey and Richardson line. Several bearings/distances are faint; no certified survey or modern geolocation made. Keep this estate's 100 acres separate from Samuel's 100-acre Buck Creek Meace purchase.

Copy signatures/acknowledgment include John/Permelia, Henry/Nancy, James/[Nancy Jane in acknowledgment], Cyrenius/Nancy Alexander, William Light. Russell County acknowledgment appears [26?] August 1848, by George Bryan deputy for William S. Patterson; day overwritten/uncertain. Pulaski recording certificate and William Light additional acknowledgment: 20 May 1850. AI text misreads dates and clerk name; use image.

Target Samuel identity probable, supported by Light–Miller–Graves and Blaze Hollow continuity with 1845 eight-acre transactions, but wife absent and original assignment date absent. Not a proof of Samuel's parents, Virginia residence, 1837 nineteen-acre acquisition, ownership of all 100 acres, or survival to 1848. Both 50-acre surveys need prior-title recovery. Original assignment itself not recovered.

story.title: Family timeline
story.introduction: Trace the Miller family from Frederick County and Baltimore to California through church registers, newspapers, and family records.

events.title: A Frederick County marriage license
events.text: Frederick County’s indexes record a license for Emanuel Miller and Rebecca Durbin. The ceremony and the bride’s identity in later Baltimore records remain open.

events.title: Charlotte Parmelia Miller is baptized
events.text: The register names Emanuel and Rebecca Miller as Charlotte’s parents and Grandmother Charlotte Miller as her sponsor.

events.title: Samuel’s household in Kentucky
events.text: The original Pulaski County census records Samuel Miller’s household.

events.title: Conflicting dates for Samuel’s death
events.text: An 1858 petition says Samuel died in Adair County around Christmas 1844. Deeds show Samuel and Huldah acknowledging sales in October 1845. His death date remains open.

events.title: Where was John Thomas born?
events.text: His death certificate gives 17 April 1851 in Washington, D.C. His daughter’s 1893 birth return also gives Washington as his birthplace. The 1860 and 1870 censuses give Maryland and Virginia. A search of available birth and baptism records found no matching entry.

events.title: Emanuel names his son John W. A.
events.text: Emanuel Miller of Stockton Alley tells the Baltimore Sun that his son John W. A. Miller, about 19, left home several weeks earlier.

events.title: John and Mary Lawson obtain a license
events.text: The District of Columbia register names John W. A. Miller and Mary M. M. Lawson. The ceremony date remains open.

events.title: A court petition names Samuel’s family
events.text: Nine children petitioned as Samuel’s heirs. The petition names Huldah as their mother.

events.title: A painter on Raborg Street
events.text: Baltimore directories list John W. A. Miller as a painter at 135 and later 129 Raborg Street.

events.title: Mary Kate Miller’s apprenticeship
events.text: An indenture names a John W. A. Miller as Mary Kate’s master. The matching initials, city, and date suggest the painter, while his identity and any kinship remain open.

events.title: Constable in Baltimore
events.text: Directories list John as a constable, first with an office at 518 West Baltimore Street and later at 660 West Baltimore Street.

events.title: John, Margaret, and John Thomas
events.text: The Baltimore census lists painter John W. Miller, Margaret, and John T. in one household. Later records support the father–son connection.

events.title: John Thomas marries Annah Bruce
events.text: John T. Miller, a Baltimore painter, married W. Anna Bruce of Piedmont. George W. Brooks officiated.

events.title: Justice of the peace
events.text: Maryland’s Senate journal records John’s appointment for Baltimore’s Fourteenth Ward on 6 May 1873. A January 1874 deed acknowledgment shows him serving as a commissioned justice.

events.title: Newspapers identify John’s siblings
events.text: Two newspapers identify Leonard D. Miller and the wife of Irvin McLaughlin as John’s siblings. Charlotte’s marriage record connects her to the McLaughlin family.

events.title: John’s death and burial
events.text: John died on 27 November at 8 East Baltimore Street and was buried at Western Cemetery on 29 November. A German-language newspaper reports a sudden death at the same address.

events.title: Margaret and the shared cemetery plot
events.text: Margaret’s death certificate names her father as Lawson. Her memorial places her in Western Cemetery plot 307-H, the same plot associated with John.

events.title: John Thomas and Annah’s household
events.text: The 1910 census records nine children born to Annah, seven still living. William and Lula appear with John and Annah in both censuses.

events.title: Annah and John Thomas die in California
events.text: Annah died in Alhambra in 1936 and John Thomas in 1938. His death certificate says he retired in 1913 after 30 years as a blacksmith.

notes.title: Emanuel named his son in 1851
notes.text: In the 28 July 1851 Baltimore Sun, Emanuel Miller of Stockton Alley said that his son John W. A. Miller, about 19, had left home. The same notice ran on 29 and 30 July. The distinctive initials and the later Baltimore reports about John’s siblings tie the son in the notice to the future justice of the peace.

notes.title: The notice helps date John’s birth
notes.text: Emanuel’s estimate points to about 1832, close to John’s age of 37 in the 1870 census. His 1877 death certificate gives age 52 and a Frederick County birthplace. The different ages and birthplaces leave his exact birth details open.

parentage.title: Rebecca Miller is a possible mother

notes.title: The baptism names Charlotte’s parents
notes.text: The 1838 baptism names Rebecca as Charlotte Parmelia Miller’s mother. The 1850 census places Charlotte with Emanuel and Rebecca, and two 1874 newspapers identify Charlotte and John as siblings. Rebecca could be John’s mother if he and Charlotte shared both parents.

notes.title: How the records identify Charlotte
notes.text: Rev. John Caspar Bucher’s register names Emanuel and Rebecca Miller as Charlotte’s parents on 5 April 1838. Charlotte P. appears with Emanuel, Rebecca, and Leonard in the 1850 Baltimore census. In 1874 newspapers identify Justice John W. A. Miller, Leonard D. Miller, and Irvin McLaughlin’s wife as siblings. Her marriage record identifies her as Charlotte Permelia Miller.

notes.title: The Durbin license leaves an identity question
notes.text: Frederick County issued a license to Emanuel Miller and Rebecca Durbin on 29 December 1830, before John’s estimated birth. The ceremony is unverified. The baptism gives Rebecca no maiden name, and the Baltimore censuses report ages that would put her at about ten in 1830 if accurate. The unnamed woman in Emanuel’s 1840 Middletown household was aged 20–29, a range broad enough to fit an older bride. The records leave open whether the license and the baptism name the same Rebecca.

notes.title: Leonard’s records give different mothers
notes.text: Maryland’s catalog describes two 1862 bounty applications as coming from Rebecca Miller, Leonard’s mother. The applications remain unread. Leonard’s 1904 death certificate names Margaret Gosset as his mother. Both leads concern Leonard, and John’s mother remains unidentified.

parentage.title: Abraham Miller in the family papers

notes.title: Two family papers preserve the Abraham tradition
notes.text: The handwritten family account and the later Family Group Record both name Abraham as John’s father. They may repeat the same tradition. Emanuel’s own statement, published during John’s lifetime, is the stronger evidence. Abraham’s place in the family remains open.

notes.title: Middletown records connect the households
notes.text: Abraham, Emanuel, and Leonard appear as separately named buyers at Adam Herring’s 1831 estate sale. Abraham and Leonard also appear on the same 1830 census page. Leonard and George Main signed Abraham’s 1836 administration bond as sureties. The sale, census, and bond place them in the same community and leave their kinship unspecified.

notes.title: The 1860 deed names six children
notes.text: A deed for Abraham’s former Middletown property names Mary M. Hedges, Jacob T. C. Miller, Daniel Miller of A., George W. Miller, Elizabeth A. Feete, and Jane A. Miller, who died without children. It omits Emanuel and John, both alive in 1860. That weighs against this Abraham as Emanuel’s father. The deed traces specific property, so an earlier transfer or another title explanation could affect that reading. Washington County’s Abraham remains a separate candidate with no identified family link.

notes.title: The grandmother named in 1838
notes.text: Charlotte’s baptism calls her sponsor Grandmother Charlotte Miller. George Main’s 1829 estate account identifies his daughter Charlotte as Leonard Miller’s wife. She is a candidate for the sponsor. The baptism leaves the grandmother’s side of the family unspecified, and Emanuel’s parents remain open.

notes.title: Another link through the Main family
notes.text: The George Main estate names Charlotte and Barbara as daughters. The Frederick equity abstract identifies Barbara’s husband as Jonathan A. Miller of Washington, D.C. The sisters connect the two Miller households by marriage. Jonathan’s relationship to Abraham remains open.

corrections.topic: 1860 Ward 18 identification of John Thomas Miller
corrections.earlier_claim: The 1860 Baltimore Ward 18 return lists Jno Miller, eight, and Thomas Miller, six, in the same numbered family as Jno W. and Margaret Miller and the McLaughlans. The older boy is the strongest childhood candidate for the John T. Miller, 18, enumerated with John W. and Margaret in 1870. This is a proposed identification. The adults’ working identification, the McLaughlin family association and the ten-year age progression favor the older boy. His reported Maryland birthplace differs from the 1870 Virginia entry and the later Washington report. The younger Thomas is unassigned and neither census states relationships.
corrections.current_assessment: On 12 November 2026 the researcher identified the eight-year-old Jno Miller on line 9 as John Thomas Miller. The John W. and Margaret household and the McLaughlin association support the identification, as does the age progression from eight in 1860 to eighteen in 1870. Both census ages are one year younger than the reported 17 April 1851 birth date implies. The 1860 return gives Maryland and the 1870 return gives Virginia, while the later death certificate reports Washington, D.C. The 1860 census supplies no relationships. The six-year-old Thomas on line 10 remains unassigned.
